lede: Rereading Borges's *Book of Imaginary Beings* at a picnic, the author dozed off and woke with an idea: many real animals are stranger than imagined ones, but our understanding is so cramped that we have "barely imagined" them.

points.h: From Borges to a bestiary for the Anthropocene
points.body:
Borges's 1967 *Book of Imaginary Beings* includes Humbaba, with lion's claws and a snake's tail; a creature Kafka imagined with a kangaroo's body and a human face; and the glowing "strong toad" of Chilean folklore. On waking, the author thought: **real animals are often stranger**, and in the Anthropocene, an age of mass extinction, they deserve a proper look.

The result is this book: a twenty-first-century bestiary in which every animal is real, and many are on the edge of extinction.

points.h: Medieval bestiaries were not just absurd
points.body:
In the thirteenth-century Ashmole Bestiary, men light a fire on an "island" that is really a whale's back; barnacle geese grow from flowers on trees; swordfish pierce and sink ships with their beaks.

But alongside the strange pictures and religious morals these books contain **sharp observation**. They did not know the limits of their own knowledge, yet they were trying to describe things as they are and to praise the beauty of existence.

points.h: A cave 30,000 years ago: we have always known ourselves through animals
points.body:
The bison, lions and rhinos in the Chauvet cave are drawn with great precision. The painters knew how animals change with the seasons: bison shedding their coats, stags in rut, salmon with the hooked jaw of the breeding season. The walls show no landscape, no sun or moon, no plants: almost nothing but animals.

The author thinks this is hard to overstate: **how humans understand themselves has always been bound up with how they see and depict other animals.** From the *Wunderkammer* (cabinet of curiosities) to the Internet is a small step.

The author says the book aims to be neither complete nor systematic. Its ordering is a little like the "Chinese encyclopedia" Borges invented, which divides animals into those belonging to the Emperor, embalmed ones, those that have just broken the flower vase, those that from a distance look like flies...

He coins a word, **aletheiagoria**: modelled on *phantasmagoria* (a magic-lantern ghost show), with the Greek *aletheia* (truth, disclosure) swapped in. It means flickering images of what is real that project a larger reality. Many of the digressions are deliberate: **thinking with animals, but not only about animals.**

- **Evolution**: understanding what can be explained makes wonder richer, not poorer. Thoreau actually measured the depth of Walden Pond with a plumb line, while his "practical" neighbours said it had no bottom. Feynman said our imagination is stretched to the utmost not to imagine things that aren't there but to comprehend those that are
- **The ocean**: about two-thirds of the book's subjects come from the sea. The ocean makes up more than 95 per cent of Earth's habitable space, yet we know little about it; during the International Geophysical Year of 1957–58, one of oceanographers' main goals was, remarkably, to study the deep sea as a dump for nuclear waste
- **The consequences of human behaviour**, and our responsibility to future generations in the Anthropocene

In the Arctic snow the author watches a heap of "fat and farting" walruses. He loves walruses: a walrus he drew on a napkin is what first won over his wife.

But for four hundred years Europeans laughed at walruses while killing them. In 1606 the crew of a Muscovy Company ship from London killed six or seven hundred adult walruses within six hours of landing. And the author's group of environmentally minded visitors, pushing forward for photos, scared the walruses back into the sea, to the captain's fury. **Each of them meant well; together they were small-time vandals.**

points.h: The A Bao A Qu: a creature never completed
points.body:
The book ends with Borges's A Bao A Qu. It lives in a tower and wakes only when a pilgrim climbs the stairs, following him up and growing more complete and more luminous; only if the climber has attained Nirvana does it reach its full form. Otherwise it stops halfway, with a moan like the rustling of silk.

The author attaches his own moral: **if we do not enlarge our imagination to take in the reality of other forms of life, we miss our main task.**

expressions.en: we have barely imagined them
expressions.zh: The source of the title: these beings are not imaginary but *barely imagined*, real creatures we have scarcely begun to picture properly.

expressions.en: the funnies
expressions.zh: "The funnies" are the comic-strip pages of a newspaper. Calling reports of ecological decline, nuclear proliferation and capitulation to torture "the funnies" is bitter irony about how bad the news is.

expressions.en: it became an obsession to the point where I could no longer avoid doing some actual work
expressions.zh: Self-mocking British humour: the obsession grew so strong that, at last, he could no longer put off doing some real work.

expressions.en: From the Wunderkammer to the Internet is a small step
expressions.zh: The step from the Renaissance cabinet of curiosities to the Internet is small: the Internet is both a servant of science and an everyday "electronic bestiary".

expressions.en: gushes up like spring water from within dark rock
expressions.zh: Curiosity about other ways of being is found in every culture, welling up like spring water from dark rock.

expressions.en: Ocean, n. A body of water occupying about two-thirds of a world made for Man – who has no gills.
expressions.zh: From Ambrose Bierce's *The Devil's Dictionary*. The joke deflates the idea that the world was made for us: most of it is ocean, and we cannot breathe there.

expressions.en: Individually well-meaning (or so we believed), we were, collectively, small-time vandals.
expressions.zh: Each of us well-meaning, or so we thought, but together we were petty vandals. "Small-time" means minor, low-level, as in "small-time crook".

expressions.en: the only genuine historical law is a law of irony
expressions.zh: Quoting John Gray: the one real law of history is irony. Science lets us remake the world to fit our values, and the world may end up a "fable" of them.

expressions.en: something like the rustling of silk
expressions.zh: The faint moan of the A Bao A Qu when it fails to reach completion, barely audible, like silk rustling.

questions: The author says that once we remake the world to fit our values, the creatures that survive will be "corollaries of our values". Can you think of animals for which this is already true?
"Everyone meant well, yet together they did damage": is there a version of the walrus story in your own life?
Do you agree that the more we understand, the more we wonder? Or can knowledge sometimes make things ordinary?

lede: With coral-like external gills and a fixed smile, the axolotl belongs to the lineage of the legendary "fire salamander". The author starts from humanity's many misunderstandings about salamanders and travels on to the move of four-legged animals onto land, the draining of the Aztec lakes, and the axolotl's power to regrow its limbs.

points.h: Salamanders in the fire: a two-thousand-year mistake
points.body:
Medieval bestiaries said the salamander could live in fire and even put it out; St Augustine used it as proof that hellfire could burn souls without consuming them. The Persian *sam andaran* means "fire within". In the Renaissance, "salamander wool" probably meant asbestos, and Francis I took the salamander in flames as his royal emblem.

Cellini recalled that when he was five his father saw a "salamander" in the fire and boxed his ears so he would never forget it. The truth is dull: **salamanders like to sleep in damp woodpiles, get thrown on the fire with the logs, and what people saw were their death throes.**

points.h: Pliny and Thomas Browne: a history of error
points.body:
Aristotle said plainly that fire-walking was only hearsay. Pliny described the Alpine salamander accurately but also said it was cold enough to put out fire and deadly poisonous. (It is simply cold-blooded and feels cool to the touch; the fire salamander's skin secretes a neurotoxin, samandarin, which may be its real "fire within".)

In the seventeenth century Thomas Browne refuted popular errors one by one in *Pseudodoxia Epidemica*. He tested it himself: a salamander placed on hot coals died at once. Yet Browne was himself obsessed with the **quincunx**, seeing God's geometry everywhere, in crystals, sea urchins, pine cones and pyramids.

In 1726 the Swiss naturalist Johann Scheuchzer found a fossil with a skull like a child's and declared it a "witness of the Flood": an accursed human from before the Deluge. This verdict held for nearly a century, until Cuvier showed in 1812 that it was not human; in 1831 it was confirmed as **an extinct giant salamander**, a relative of the giant salamanders living today in the rivers of China and Japan.

The philosopher James McCosh even called it a "type" foreshadowing the "perfect type" of man. The author says no one speaks of "perfect types" any more, but amphibian fossils really do foreshadow most of our body's structure.

points.h: Absurd theories that put humans at the centre
points.body:
That the human brain evolved in a relatively short time is so counterintuitive that some looked for alternatives:
- In 1919 the anthropologist Frederic Wood Jones claimed big-brained proto-humans had existed for tens of millions of years, looking something like tarsiers
- Stranger still was the "initial bipedalism" hypothesis: the humanoid form came before fish, humans are the prototype of all vertebrates, and every other animal evolved from us. Our ancestors floated upright in the water like champagne corks, with axolotl-like gills on their necks

The author's verdict: absurd, but at least splendidly and originally so.

The author invites you to travel back some 365 million years. The air is only 15 per cent oxygen and you feel a little dizzy; on the shore stand eight-metre "giant fungi", *Prototaxites*; there are no flying insects, let alone birdsong. In the murky water is something the size of a ten-year-old child with seven toes on each foot: ***Ichthyostega***, possibly a common ancestor of us and the salamanders. It sees you and is gone with a ripple.

The key point: **lungs and limbs appeared first, while animals still lived entirely in water**, not by crawling up the shore first like mudskippers.

points.h: The lost dynasty of the amphibians
points.body:
For more than a hundred million years across the Carboniferous and Permian, amphibians were the top predators on land: the nine-metre, crocodile-like *Prionosuchus*, and *Diplocaulus* with its boomerang-shaped head. Later the amniotes (reptiles and mammals) took over, "**which is probably why this book was not written by a large frog**".

Today's amphibians are just as strange: the "toad from hell", the purple frog that looks like a bag of jelly, the gastric-brooding frog (now extinct) that swallowed its eggs and raised them in its stomach. On current trends we face the greatest extinction of amphibians since the Permian.

The name axolotl may come from Xolotl, the Aztec god of fire and guide of the dead, or from the Nahuatl words for "water" and "dog". It keeps its larval form all its life yet can breed. This is called **neoteny**. Humans have about twenty neotenous traits too.

Julian Huxley injected axolotls with hormone and turned them into a land-dwelling form like the tiger salamander. His brother Aldous Huxley imagined from this that a human who lived indefinitely would turn back into a hunched, hairy ape.

points.h: "Ontogeny recapitulates phylogeny" and its dark side
points.body:
In 1866 Ernst Haeckel proposed that every embryo replays the whole history of life. The theory suited the European idea of "progress" at the time and was used to prop up **scientific racism**: European children were equivalent to the adults of "primitive peoples". Freud adopted it, and Sándor Ferenczi wrote a book arguing that the human longing to return to the womb is a longing for the sea.

The axolotl entered European knowledge right at the start of European expansion: the Spanish conquest of Mexico.

In 1519 Cortés saw Tenochtitlan on its lake, "like an enchanted vision". The Aztecs' floating gardens (*chinampas*) were highly productive, and axolotls were on the menu. The conquerors' strongest weapon was **smallpox**: "guns, germs and steel, but the greatest of these is germs".

Afterwards the lakes of the Valley of Mexico were drained. Lake Chalco flowed away through a giant tunnel, and Lake Xochimilco is reduced to a few polluted canals. Neoteny once gave the axolotl an edge in highland lakes; now it is a fatal weakness. **It survives mainly because humans find it cute and useful for research.**

points.h: Regeneration: a clue to the fire of life
points.body:
An axolotl can regrow a lost limb completely, as many times as needed, without scarring; it can also regenerate eyes and parts of its brain. The wound first becomes a layer of signalling cells, then fibroblasts migrate and gather into a **blastema**, which grows the new limb. Remarkably, wherever the cut is made, it regrows only the missing part.

The ending: people believed salamanders held the secret of fire, which was not true; but the axolotl may hold clues to **the fire of life**.

expressions.en: ‘ludicrous fish’
expressions.zh: One of the first European names for the animal was *piscis ludicrous*, the "ludicrous fish": in the old sense, comic or laughable.

expressions.en: a Nike swoosh for Francois I
expressions.zh: The salamander in flames was Francis I's royal emblem; calling it his "Nike swoosh" maps a Renaissance badge onto a modern brand logo.

expressions.en: The Renaissance artist, sexual predator and murderer Benvenuto Cellini
expressions.zh: Three titles strung together in one phrase, a deadpan way of summing up Cellini's whole character, the art and the crimes alike.

expressions.en: what’s a ventricle between friends?
expressions.zh: A salamander heart has three chambers and ours has four. The joke plays on the phrase "what's a few dollars between friends?", meaning such a small difference hardly matters.

expressions.en: which is probably why this book was not written by a large frog
expressions.zh: Amphibians lost their dominance to the amniotes, "which is probably why this book was not written by a large frog": a comic way of saying we descend from the winners.

expressions.en: If this theory is absurd it is at least splendidly and originally so.
expressions.zh: A memorable backhanded compliment: if the theory is nonsense, at least it is magnificent, original nonsense.

expressions.en: So abideth these three: guns, germs and steel; but the greatest of these is germs.
expressions.zh: A mash-up of 1 Corinthians 13:13 ("faith, hope, charity... but the greatest of these is charity") with the title of Jared Diamond's *Guns, Germs, and Steel*. Disease did more than weapons to defeat the Aztecs.

expressions.en: it finally gurgled away like water down a plughole
expressions.zh: Lake Chalco finally drained away with a gurgle like bathwater going down a plughole, extending the earlier image of the valley as the bottom of a bathtub.

expressions.en: Behold … Lo … Hail … Ave
expressions.zh: Archaic exclamations used to introduce strange amphibians, parodying the hymn-like voice of Christopher Smart's poems praising all creatures.

questions: The axolotl is nearly extinct in the wild but breeds in huge numbers in labs and aquariums because it is cute and scientifically useful. Does surviving that way count as being "saved"?
Cellini's sighting of a "salamander" in the fire seemed to confirm the legend. Are there similar cases today, where a real observation is read through existing beliefs as something else?
Haeckel's recapitulation theory was used to support racism. When a scientific theory is abused, does the responsibility lie with the theory or with those who use it?

lede: No eyes, no mouth, no organs, no movement: a sponge hardly looks like an animal. The author sets out to show that the lumpy barrel sponge is a subtle piece of design, and a talisman for the emergence of all multicellular animals, ourselves included.

points.body: A prettier candidate would be the Venus's flower basket, whose glassy skeleton looks like lace. A pair of young shrimps swim inside, grow too big to leave, and spend their lives trapped there; in Japan it symbolizes eternal love. The author instead chooses the misfit at the other end: the barrel sponge, coloured like a bruise in pale purple, dark red and greyish brown, big enough for a diver to climb inside (but please don't: it harms the sponge).

points.h: Not symmetrical, so not an animal?
points.body:
Thomas Browne believed animals must have a top and bottom, front and back, so he doubted that "two-headed snakes" could exist. Modern classification likewise calls bilaterally and radially symmetrical animals "Eumetazoa" (true animals), while asymmetrical sponges are admitted to the animal kingdom only grudgingly as "Parazoa" (beside animals).

The author sets this beside a photograph of Joseph Merrick, the Elephant Man: look closely, and from the deformed face one calm, clear eye looks back. **A little more attention lets us see the extraordinary in what prejudice calls ugly.**

points.h: A filter-feeding machine that uses the chimney effect
points.body:
Water near the seabed moves slowly and water a little higher moves faster, so the outflow opening at the top of a barrel sponge (the *osculum*, "little mouth") works like a chimney. Put a drop of dye at its base and coloured water puffs out of the top like smoke from a steam train.

Its thousands of tiny chambers are lined with **choanocytes** (collar cells), whose flagella beat in unison, drawing in bacteria and expelling waste.

points.h: A creature of the moon, the sun and plants
points.body:
Using the difference in current speed amounts to using tidal energy from the pull of the moon and sun. Sponges in shallow water also host algae inside them, which "pay the rent" in oxygen and nutrients, often in such surplus that the surrounding ecosystem benefits. Some sponges pipe light deep into their bodies through transparent tubes to feed the algae: the only animals known to do so.

Some barrel sponges may live two thousand years, as old as California's redwoods. Around 160 million years ago a sponge reef stretched from Spain to Romania, bigger than today's Great Barrier Reef.

In 1907 it was found that if certain sponges are pressed through a very fine mesh and broken into single cells, the cells can reassemble into a complete animal.

More importantly, sponge collar cells are almost identical to single-celled **choanoflagellates**, and the genes choanoflagellates use to stick cells together closely resemble the equivalent genes in all multicellular animals, so we almost certainly evolved from them. A sponge has fewer than a dozen more specialized cell types than a colony of choanoflagellates, which makes it a good model for **the earliest multicellular animals**.

- Slime moulds with no neurons can remember the pattern of events
- In swarms, *Noctiluca* can light up a whole stretch of sea
- Foraminifera choose sand grains of particular colours and shapes to glue onto their shells
- *Tetrahymena thermophila* has seven sexes and can mate with any but its own, giving it twenty-one "sexual orientations"

In 1795 James Hutton said the Earth showed "no vestige of a beginning, no prospect of an end". Deep time made Darwin's theory possible but also left "Darwin's dilemma": Cambrian fossils appear already complex and diverse. The answer lies in the long Proterozoic before it. Eukaryotes may have appeared 2.7 billion years ago, went through the "boring billion", and sponge-like multicellular life may have appeared around 900 million years ago.

Analogies (if Earth's history were a day, humans would appear three seconds before midnight) help us think but do not necessarily help us feel. The author suggests walking and meditating on the Archaean rocks of north-west Scotland.

points.h: Microbes are the cake, we are the icing
points.body:
Respiration, photosynthesis and fermentation were all invented by microbes, along with chemosynthesis, which we never learned. As the palaeontologist Andrew Knoll puts it: **"Eukaryotes are the icing, prokaryotes are the cake."** Even death is just "being metabolically different".

So are we just froth on a great vat of microbes? The author borrows Einstein's reply: you could describe Beethoven's Ninth in mathematics, "but what would be the point?" Prokaryotes are the original notes; eukaryotes play new melodies and harmonies from them.

The demosponges are the oldest living multicellular animals with a clear trace, going back to the "Snowball Earth" period. All other multicellular animals were probably early offshoots of them.

Next time you see a sponge, consider that **your direct ancestors were more like it than like you**. It is we who depend on processes it pioneered, so the real *spongers* (freeloaders, people living off others) are us.

expressions.en: a person who is always asking for money
expressions.zh: A *sponge* or *sponger* is also someone who always asks for money or lives off others. The chapter returns to this double meaning in its final line.

expressions.en: a group of wonky giants
expressions.zh: A cluster of lopsided giants. *Wonky* is British slang for crooked, unsteady or not quite right.

expressions.en: a ‘wastebasket taxon’
expressions.zh: A "wastebasket taxon" is a category where biologists dump organisms that fit nowhere else.

expressions.en: which pay the rent with oxygen and metabolites
expressions.zh: The algae "pay the rent" with oxygen and metabolic products: a domestic image for symbiosis between lodger and host.

expressions.en: a submarine instance of ‘rainbow body’
expressions.zh: Borrowing the Tibetan Buddhist idea of the "rainbow body", in which light passes through the body unhindered. Yogis aspire to it, but a supposedly "lower" animal got there first, under the sea.

expressions.en: the amazing performing fleas in the big top of life
expressions.zh: Bacteria and archaea as the star flea circus in the big top of life: tiny performers that are the real virtuosos of metabolism.

expressions.en: death is not the end, it’s just a case of being metabolically different
expressions.zh: Death is not the end, just "being metabolically different", a deadpan line from the microbe's point of view, where the dead body simply becomes food for other metabolisms.

expressions.en: From Hallucigenia to Kim Jong-un
expressions.zh: From a weird Cambrian creature (*Hallucigenia*) to the North Korean leader: an absurdly wide span to convey the range of animal forms.

expressions.en: it is we, not it, who are the spongers
expressions.zh: The closing pun: we, not the sponge, are the freeloaders, living off the processes it pioneered.

questions: The author uses a photograph of the Elephant Man to discuss how we see "ugly" creatures. Do you think the comparison is apt?
If life is essentially a great vat of microbes and we are only the froth on top, does that make you feel small, or does it make things more interesting?
Do you have a way of really feeling deep time, rather than just understanding the numbers?

lede: Anus on top, mouth underneath, covered in venomous spines, it pushes its stomach out of its body to digest coral. The media once cast the crown-of-thorns starfish as a doomsday monster devouring the reefs, but the real monster was behind the scenes all along: us.

points.h: A predator with its anus on top
points.body:
The author opens with William Burroughs's story of "the man who taught his asshole to talk": reality can be as weird as his imagination. The crown-of-thorns starfish has no head. Its anus is on top and its mouth is at the centre of its underside. That made sense for ancestors that ate debris on the seabed; its distant relatives the sea cucumbers still "graze" in herds on the abyssal plains.

But the crown-of-thorns switched to eating live coral. It glides on thousands of tube feet at about the speed of a clock's minute hand, wraps itself over the coral, **turns one of its stomachs out through its mouth**, and pours out digestive juices that reduce the polyps to a paste it then sucks back up. In swarms it can destroy a stretch of reef in days.

Few people had seen it before, and it was thought to be rare. Then an outbreak erupted around a tourist island on the Great Barrier Reef, and reports came in from across the Indo-Pacific. *The New York Times* quoted conservationists saying it might be "a catastrophe unparalleled in human history"; *The Economist* said the whole region's economy could collapse along with the reefs.

Then the numbers fell sharply and many reefs recovered. People came to appreciate again **how resilient reefs are, and how patchy our knowledge is**.

As in a B monster movie, or *Beowulf*, the greater horror was still to come: by the early twenty-first century scientists were warning that unless emissions were cut drastically, **global warming and ocean acidification** would destroy the remaining reefs within a century.

points.h: From cabinet of curiosities to "living world"
points.body:
Humans have lived alongside forests, grasslands and riverbanks for hundreds of thousands of years, but our feel for the tropical underwater world is new and shallow. In the early eighteenth century Georg Rumphius, "the blind seer of Ambon", described hundreds of sea creatures precisely in *The Ambonese Curiosity Cabinet*, including the crown-of-thorns (its sting "burns fiercely, so that no one wants to touch it").

But cataloguing could not explain how these lives were connected. In the 1830s Darwin proposed that **atolls grow on slowly sinking seamounts**: corals keep growing upward to stay near the sunlight, building structures thousands of times larger than the pyramids. The hypothesis was not confirmed until the 1950s.

points.h: The diving age: discovery and destruction at once
points.body:
Alfred Russel Wallace was overwhelmed by the beauty of the reef in Ambon Bay: "the reality exceeded the most glowing descriptions I had ever read." After the Second World War, scuba diving let thousands of ordinary people see it for themselves. Coral reefs cover less than 1 per cent of the ocean yet hold about a quarter of its biodiversity.

But the moment we discovered the reefs was also the moment we watched them being destroyed: many reefs in South-East Asia and the Caribbean have been almost wiped out by overfishing and pollution. **The damage done by humanity as a whole far exceeds anything a rampaging starfish could do.**

The earliest starfish fossils date from the Ordovician, when fish had no jaws yet and sea scorpions the size of basketball players lurked in the mud. The ancestors of echinoderms were originally **bilaterally symmetrical**; they later fixed themselves to the seabed and became radially symmetrical. The ancestors of starfish then let go of the seabed and began to move, but kept their radial symmetry.

Starfish larvae are bilaterally symmetrical; as they mature, the left half of the body absorbs the right half and the animal grows into five rays. Sea cucumbers go from bilateral to five-fold and then, as adults, back to bilateral: stranger than Ovid's *Metamorphoses*, and a sign that Haeckel's recapitulation theory explains only a small part of the animal kingdom.

points.h: No brain, but it can see
points.body:
Starfish come in many forms: the armless "pincushion starfish", *Zoroaster* with arms like elephants' trunks, the sunflower star a metre across with 16 to 24 soft arms. Among the brittle stars, the "Gorgon's head" really does look like a tangle of snakes.

Echinoderms have no brain, only a nerve net spread through the body, but each arm ends in a light-sensitive eyespot. One brittle star is covered in lenses made of calcite crystals that may together work like a single huge compound eye, a material previously known only from trilobites. **We can, literally, be seen by stars.**

Under current pressures most coral reefs may face destruction around 2050, something not seen for 55 million years. But it is not hopeless: once other pressures are removed, reefs can recover within decades even from a direct hit by a hydrogen bomb, so marine protected areas are worth trying.

Starfish are tough. They have survived three mass extinctions: the end-Ordovician, the end-Permian (when 96 per cent of marine species died) and the end-Cretaceous. **In the distant future, starfish will probably be around to bury us**, and there will be new species stranger than the crown-of-thorns.

expressions.en: If you look into infinity what do you see? Your backside!
expressions.zh: The chapter's epigraph, from the Dada artist Tristan Tzara: gaze into infinity and what do you see? Your own backside. It anticipates the starfish whose anus faces the sky.

expressions.en: the night-soil men of the deep in a holothurian heaven
expressions.zh: Sea cucumbers as the "night-soil men" of the deep, and the abyssal plain as their paradise. *Night soil* is the old term for human excrement collected from privies at night.

expressions.en: a submarine version of Pinhead
expressions.zh: A starfish bristling with venomous spines is an undersea Pinhead, the nail-studded demon of the horror film *Hellraiser*.

expressions.en: Gliding along about as fast as the minute hand on a clock
expressions.zh: It glides at roughly the speed of a clock's minute hand: movement too slow to see, but enough to destroy a reef.

expressions.en: And thereby hangs a true tale
expressions.zh: A play on Shakespeare's stock phrase "thereby hangs a tale" (there's a story behind that), with *true* added because the story that follows really happened.

expressions.en: the edge of terror
expressions.zh: The author mocks his own poor diving skills: on his first dive he was never far from "the edge of terror".

expressions.en: ‘if you dive here you may see some truly horrible things before you dissolve’
expressions.zh: Black humour from a travel guide: in some Philippine waters you might see truly horrible things before you yourself dissolve in chemicals and human waste.

expressions.en: like courtesans in feather boas
expressions.zh: Slender brittle stars draped over the coral like courtesans in feather boas: an image of languid, frilly elegance.

expressions.en: We can, literally, be seen by stars
expressions.zh: A literal pun: starfish and brittle stars are "stars" in English, and some of them can see, so we really can be seen by stars.

expressions.en: starfish should be around to bury us
expressions.zh: Starfish have outlasted three mass extinctions, so they will probably still be here to bury us: a wry reversal of who outlives whom.

questions: The 1960s starfish panic turned out to be exaggerated, and some people treat climate warnings as another case of crying wolf. How can we tell the two kinds of warning apart?
Coral reefs were destroyed even as we "discovered" them. Can watching and tourism themselves be a form of damage?
An animal without a brain can still "see". Does that change how you understand perception?

lede: Near a remote ocean island the author once watched wild dolphins perform, and the joy of it changed his sense of being alive, the way a narrow escape from death does. This chapter asks: what kind of beings are dolphins, and what does the answer mean for how we treat them?

points.body: Say "dolphin" and people think of the bottlenose, the easiest to train. In fact there are nearly forty species, from the smallest, the Maui's dolphin, the size of a wild boar, to the largest, the orca, the size of a bus. The common dolphin is slate grey on the back and mustard yellow on the sides, like the camouflage on a First World War warship; the dusky dolphin's black-and-white markings look like intertwined flames; the hourglass dolphin's white bands look as if a giant thumb and forefinger had pinched its waist.

points.h: Humans and dolphins: perhaps cooperation came first
points.body:
Early humans foraging along the coast probably watched dolphins drive shoals of fish toward the shore, and learned to cooperate with them. Pliny the Elder recorded people in southern France fishing for mullet together with dolphins: "the dolphins do not fear man as something alien."
- The Wurundjeri people of Australia held dolphins sacred, took only the fish the dolphins did not need, and believed the souls of the dead became dolphins that guarded their families
- Aristotle said Greek boys and dolphins formed deep attachments
- In Minoan frescoes 3,500 years old, dolphins appear alongside running deer; Apollo took the form of a dolphin to found the oracle at Delphi (Delphi takes its name from the dolphin)

The town of Taiji in Japan slaughters thousands of dolphins each year and sells those caught alive to aquariums (*The Cove*). Less visible are the tens or hundreds of thousands of dolphins that die each year as bycatch in fishing nets, while mercury and PCB pollution also harm them.

Covering all this up are the trained dolphins performing in aquariums, whose "smile" is as misleading as their situation: **it is only the shape of the mouth, not an expression.**

The philosopher Thomas White argues that dolphins are **non-human persons**: different enough to be regarded as an alien intelligence, but with dignity all the same, so mistreating them is indefensible.

The maverick John Lilly said something similar long before. He took psychedelics with Timothy Leary and Allen Ginsberg, wanted to build a floating living room where humans and wild dolphins could talk at any time, and proposed a seat at the United Nations for a "Cetacean Nation". Some of his claims lacked data, but most of his intuitions about dolphin intelligence, communication and emotion were later confirmed.

Aristotle knew dolphins were mammals. He recorded a school of dolphins waiting in a harbour until fishermen released an injured companion, and dolphins holding up a dead calf. These behaviours seem credible today; he only exaggerated how high they leap.

Modern research has added much more. Dolphins' sex lives are as rich as bonobos': they court all year and use beaks, flippers and tails. Spinner dolphins have group orgies of a dozen or more ("wuzzles"), and male bottlenoses have even tried to mate with sharks and turtles.

The ancestors of whales and dolphins looked like a cross between a wolf and a nimble hippo. Orcas lunge onto beaches to seize seal pups, and sometimes toss them about like a cat playing with a mouse. They hunt so efficiently that they need to "work" only a few hours a day and have lots of time to socialize.

Dolphins also gang up to coerce females and kill other dolphins' calves, but on the whole they are superb cooperators: mothers use "baby talk", let calves ride in their slipstream and babysit for one another. **Each dolphin has its own signature whistle, which companions imitate to call it: in effect, a name.** When playing games with people, they make allowances for our poor swimming.

Dolphins make clicks lasting less than a thousandth of a second in air sacs below the blowhole. These are projected through a parabolic dish at the front of the skull and through the "melon", which can change shape like a lens; echoes travel through the lower jaw to the inner ear. They click 8 to 2,000 times a second, never sending the next click before the last echo returns.

They can "see" a beating heart and a foetus inside a human body, and are said to detect pregnancy before the woman herself knows. From ten metres away they can distinguish differences in thickness of a few hundredths of a millimetre, equivalent to separating echoes less than a millionth of a second apart. The blind boy Ben Underwood found his way around streets by clicking his tongue; the deaf percussionist Evelyn Glennie feels vibrations with her body; **dolphins routinely do more than either.**

One study identified 186 kinds of whistle. Captive bottlenoses have learned more than sixty human signals and can understand about 2,000 sentences. Carl Sagan remarked that some dolphins are said to have learned English, but no human has been reported to have learned "dolphinese".

Heidegger held that only humans are "world-forming" and animals are "poor in world". The author thinks dolphins unsettle that view: mental representation comes before language; dolphins, like us, are "dependent rational animals", and they excel at the "simple" things that ultimately make humans happy too, such as endless play. **In the beginning, perhaps, was not the word but the gesture.**

Hume said people resonate with each other like strings of equal length and tension. In the midst of plague and betrayal, Boccaccio wrote: **to have compassion for the afflicted is a human thing.** Dolphins show us the possibility of friendship and hope, which Epicurus thought might be the greatest virtue, though he was not thinking of another species.

expressions.en: I felt as if reborn, my body made of sunlight
expressions.zh: Reaching harbour safely after a storm, the author felt reborn, as if his body were made of sunlight: the euphoria of survival.

expressions.en: curvaceous and muted variants of the dazzle camouflage
expressions.zh: The common dolphin's markings are a softer, curvier version of the "dazzle camouflage" painted on First World War ships to confuse the enemy's eye.

expressions.en: denatured, shrink-wrapped slaves
expressions.zh: Performing aquarium dolphins as slaves stripped of their nature and packaged for sale. *Denatured* means altered so as to lose natural properties, as in denatured alcohol; *shrink-wrapped* evokes supermarket packaging.

expressions.en: as well as how bad web-page design could be a dozen years ago
expressions.zh: The swirling pink and purple blobs on Lilly's website recall the psychedelics he took, and also, the author adds drily, how bad web design was a dozen years ago.

expressions.en: clad in shorts much too small for a man of his age
expressions.zh: A deadpan aside: in the film, George C. Scott wears shorts far too small for a man his age.

expressions.en: Wonko the Sane
expressions.zh: In Douglas Adams's *Hitchhiker's Guide* books, Wonko the Sane lives in a house turned inside out, an "asylum" that keeps the rest of the world locked in. The author suggests it may be the most fitting satire of Lilly.

expressions.en: the equivalent of a child going ‘wheeee!’
expressions.zh: The flat whistle dolphins make while bow-riding is the equivalent of a child shouting "wheeee!": pure play.

expressions.en: In the beginning, perhaps, was not the word but the gesture.
expressions.zh: A rewrite of the opening of John's Gospel, "In the beginning was the Word": perhaps meaning began with gesture, not language.

expressions.en: umana cosa é aver compassione degli afflitti
expressions.zh: From the preface to Boccaccio's *Decameron*: "it is a human thing to have compassion for the afflicted."

questions: If dolphins are "non-human persons", should dolphin shows in aquariums be banned? Do ordinary tourists who go to watch bear any responsibility?
Dolphins make allowances for human clumsiness, yet they also gang up to coerce females and kill calves. How do these two sides affect your view of the "dolphins are angels" image?
For a creature that "sees" the world through sound, "language" may be entirely unlike ours. Do you think humans could ever truly understand it?

lede: Gaping mouth, dead-fish eyes, limbless writhing: moray eels give people the creeps. The author moves from eels to how imagined monsters have changed over time, from deep-sea creatures and the white whale to the atom bomb, aliens and zombies, with the monsters coming ever closer to us.

points.body:
The snowflake moray has delicate markings and is popular with aquarium keepers; it is harmless as long as you leave it alone and don't drink its toxic blood. Its genus name *Echidna* comes from Hesiod's monster, half nymph and half giant serpent.

People fear morays partly because they look like snakes and partly because their mouths are always open. The author thinks there is more: **the bulging, unblinking eyes are like a corpse's, and the limbless swimming is disturbingly sensual.**

Aristotle thought eels arose from earthworms generated spontaneously in mud. Only in 1777 was it proved that eels are fish. As a young medical student, Freud dissected hundreds looking for male sex organs and finally gave up. In 1896 Giovanni Grassi watched the transparent, leaf-shaped **leptocephalus** turn into a glass eel, proving they were the same species, and the following year identified a frilly ribbon as the testes.

In 1922 Johannes Schmidt found that European eels are born in the **Sargasso Sea**, up to 7,000 kilometres away. Mature silver eels swim back to the Sargasso to spawn, and the larvae drift back to Europe on the currents, passing through the glass eel, elver and yellow eel stages to become silver eels. Their journey is as epic as the salmon's, only in the opposite direction, and **many of the transformations are still not understood**.

The true eels number about 600 species: duckbill eels (one called the "black sorcerer"), an eel with a beak like an avocet's, deep-sea cutthroat eels whose larvae have telescope eyes, the "rusty spaghetti eel", the frog-headed eel. Garden eels stand in colonies in the sand and all retract at once at the first sign of danger, **like the horns of a thousand snails recoiling at a distant vibration**.

Then there are creatures that look like eels but are not: the electric eel (closer to catfish), the wolf eel, the gulper eel that lures prey with a glowing tail, the frilled shark, and the hagfish: blind, jawless, with four hearts, squirting slime, and fond of burrowing into corpses through the anus and eating them hollow.

points.h: The moray's second set of jaws
points.body:
There are about two hundred moray species, with tiger, dragon and giraffe patterns (the giraffe moray's markings look like... you guessed it), and the ribbon eel, whose males are electric blue when young and which turns yellow and female in old age. Cleaner shrimps dart in and out of a moray's mouth like ballet dancers in the jaws of a mechanical stage dragon.

With its mouth always open and its visible jaws small and weak, how does it feed? Only in 2006 was it observed: **deep in the throat is a second set of pharyngeal jaws** that shoots forward at high speed, seizes the prey and drags it into the gullet. Nothing else in the world is like this; the closest thing is the creature in the film *Alien*, designed to provoke maximum fear and disgust.

As dangerous animals recede further from our experience, imagined monsters change shape. Today the most dangerous animals to humans are, overwhelmingly, other humans.

A hundred years ago the nature writer Richard Jefferies looked at the more than 4,000 new species dredged from the deep by the *Challenger* expedition and saw only "malformations that startle the mind". The passage appears in a memoir full of transcendent joy; he later wrote a novel imagining London swallowed by flood and wilderness, and the deep-sea monsters may have been a projection of his fear of industrialization.

points.h: The white whale and the atom bomb
points.body:
In Melville's *Moby-Dick*, the real destructive force is Captain Ahab's obsession. In 1923 D. H. Lawrence read its moral: "a maniac captain of the soul, and three eminently practical mates... all the practicality turned to the mad chase... That's America!" The whiteness of the whale foreshadowed the doom of industrial civilization.

Twenty-two years later came the atom bomb. The official reporter of the Nagasaki bombing wrote that the fireball was "a living thing, a new species of being, born right before our incredulous eyes". But the enormity of nuclear war could not be imagined, and Godzilla and the giant ants of *Them!* now look as quaint as the medieval unicorn and manticore.

*Alien* has been read as expressing fear of pollution, pesticides and carcinogens: the self mutating into a monster. The early twenty-first-century vogue for zombies and vampires, "half-humans" or degraded humans, answers fears of overpopulation, famine, pandemics and climate change.

The author sees an upside: **placing monsters as close to humans as the jugular vein lets other animals off the hook**, so we can see them as themselves rather than as metaphors for something else. Deep-sea creatures' faces were never "designed" to be looked at by anything on land; learning a little about their evolution can turn horror into wonder.

The moray embodies two things:
- Its two sets of jaws show that the struggle to survive can produce astonishing novelty: from the first "toothed terror", the arrow worm, to hagfish and lampreys, then jawed fish, and us
- The snake-like side-to-side wriggle is one of the most efficient forms of movement animals have invented, carried on for more than five hundred million years from conodonts and hagfish to snakes, which appeared only tens of millions of years ago. **This flame-like undulation may be older than earthly fire**: always changing and always continuing, an image of life itself

expressions.en: Compared to this, the Snowflake and other Moray eels are pussycats.
expressions.zh: Compared with the mythical monster, the snowflake and other morays are pussycats. A *pussycat* is someone or something gentle and harmless despite appearances.

expressions.en: Saltwater eels are uncanny.
expressions.zh: *Uncanny* means strangely familiar and unsettling at once; it is also Freud's concept of *das Unheimliche*, which links neatly to his eel dissections later in the chapter.

expressions.en: like the horns of a thousand snails recoiling to a distant vibration
expressions.zh: Garden eels pulling back into the sand all at once, like a thousand snails' horns retracting at a faraway tremor.

expressions.en: The Giraffe moray has markings very like those of . . . you guessed it.
expressions.zh: A joke left deliberately unfinished: the giraffe moray's pattern resembles, of course, a giraffe's.

expressions.en: like ballet dancers in the jaws of a mechanical stage dragon
expressions.zh: Cleaner shrimps working inside a moray's mouth like ballerinas dancing inside the jaws of a mechanical dragon on stage.

expressions.en: Inchoate fears have vested in new forms.
expressions.zh: Vague, unformed fears have attached themselves to new shapes. *Inchoate* means just begun, not yet fully formed.

expressions.en: ‘unthinkable’ but never undo-able
expressions.zh: Nuclear war is called "unthinkable", yet once it happens it can never be undone: a pointed contrast between two near-rhyming words.

expressions.en: as close to humans as the jugular vein
expressions.zh: Monsters kept just a jugular vein away from us, echoing vampires and zombies that go for the neck, and the Quran's line that God is "nearer to him than his jugular vein".

expressions.en: let other animals off the hook
expressions.zh: To *let someone off the hook* is to release them from blame or obligation: other animals no longer have to carry the role of monster.

expressions.en: a wriggling, rippling, flame-like motion that may be older than earthly fire
expressions.zh: That writhing, rippling, flame-like movement may be older than fire on Earth: an image of life as a flame that has never gone out.

questions: The author says that as monsters become more human (zombies, vampires), this is good news for other animals. Do you agree?
What do you think is the most typical "monster" of our time? What fear does it reflect?
European eels travel thousands of kilometres to spawn in the Sargasso Sea, and many details remain a mystery. What else that science knows still strikes you as mysterious?

lede: "We are all worms," said Churchill, "but I do believe that I am a glow-worm." The author invites us to step past the threshold of disgust and look at the motley worms that have flourished since the Cambrian, ending with flatworms as a way into parasitism, death and the miracle of life.

points.body: The geneticist Steve Jones put it this way: **however grand, each of us is a ten-metre tube through which food flows, mostly in one direction.** Our attitude to worms is much as it was when bestiaries were written seven hundred years ago: the ones in the soil are good, and the rest are best avoided. The author says this makes us miss a great many beautiful, horrifying and wonderful things: arrow worms, spoon worms, peanut worms, "penis worms"...

points.h: The Cambrian explosion had a long fuse
points.body:
For more than a hundred million years before the Cambrian, life was already experimenting with ways of "getting big". One was the sponge; another was the Ediacaran biota: the fractal, frond-like *Charnia*, the ribbed, cushion-like *Dickinsonia*, and *Tribrachidium*, like a triskelion on a pizza. But they probably left no descendants.

The Cambrian explosion may have come from rising oxygen, an arms race set off by the appearance of eyes, and **a "toothed terror" with a through-gut and an anus**, able to eat, digest and excrete the world more efficiently than any animal before. The author says that much of the later history of life is a footnote to this leap.

- The first "toothed terror" may have been the arrow worm
- Fossils of priapulids (penis worms) look like "novelty condoms with organs inside"
- *Hallucigenia* was first reconstructed upside down: it was thought to walk on stilt-like spines and wave tentacles on its back, but the tentacles were legs and the spines were on its back
- *Hallucigenia* may be a relative of the **velvet worm**. Today's velvet worms live in groups with hierarchies, hunt cooperatively, the males insert an organ on their heads into the female, and they squirt slime at enemies; they look very like the 540-million-year-old fossils

Nematodes may be the most diverse and numerous worms: *H. mephisto* lives in a gold mine nearly 3,000 metres underground. *Caenorhabditis elegans* has only about 300 neurons; it was the first animal to have its genome sequenced and its nervous system fully mapped, and has helped earn at least four Nobel Prizes, **doing a great deal with very little and truly living up to the name *elegans***.

The annelids include earthworms, the tubeworms and Pompeii worms of deep-sea vents, and Christmas tree worms, which *Avatar* enlarged and transplanted to Pandora. Darwin studied the earthworms in his garden and found that **earthworms make the soil**; when plugging their burrows they even choose leaves sensibly by shape.

Flatworms have no body cavity: "its insides have no inside". They have to be flat, relying on diffusion to move oxygen and nutrients. But they actually belong to two phyla with three ways of life, and the differences are as great as the similarities. The author says this is a reminder that **language that is too coarse hides huge differences and detail.**

The acoel *Convoluta roscoffensis* swallows green algae when young and never feeds again, living on the algae's photosynthesis. At low tide thousands rise to the surface of the sand to sunbathe; put in a laboratory tank, they still seek the sunlight twice a day. Rachel Carson wrote that, with no brain, it "remembers, in every fibre of its small green body, the tidal rhythm of the distant sea".

Some flatworms have a pair of goofy little eyes and may be the cutest worms of all. Their lack of a body cavity is a later loss: they gave up the cavity, as humans gave up fur and tails. Some mimic the bright patterns of poisonous sea slugs.

They are hermaphrodites and practise **"penis fencing"**: using two penises on their front as weapons, each tries to stab the other and fertilize it, combining two of humanity's favourite things, sex and fighting.

More than half of all flatworms are parasites, and schistosomiasis is the most serious parasitic disease after malaria. Fear of parasites has adaptive value, but it can also become an illness (delusional parasitosis) or be exploited politically: the Nazis likened Jews to parasites.

The author says "appreciating" can mean understanding better rather than liking:
- In some ecosystems parasites have twenty times the biomass of the top predators; plenty of parasites is often a sign of ecological health
- *Toxoplasma* knows how to enter precise circuits in a rat's amygdala so that it loses its fear of cat smell, and **in some respects understands the mammalian brain better than neuroscientists do**
- One hypothesis holds that parasites drove the evolution and persistence of sexual reproduction

The anthropologist Scott Atran calls it "the tragedy of cognition": language makes us aware of others who are absent, and also makes death a silent interlocutor in our heads. The author suggests trying on different views of death, the way marine flatworms try on different colours:
- After losing his daughter, Cicero found Stoic "indifference" wholly inadequate: "They tear us, they burn us, and you tell us to forget?"
- Bertrand Russell urged building the soul's habitation "on the firm foundation of unyielding despair", yet in old age he still drove the Russell–Einstein Manifesto
- The Earth system scientist Tyler Volk: without death the biosphere would be about two hundred times less productive; our bodies too must become tilth
- Hume's humour on his deathbed; Karel Čapek said a gardener does not become a butterfly when he dies but an earthworm, "tasting all the dark, nitrogenous, spicy delights of the soil"

The ending: a single cell can regenerate a whole planarian. **That is proof enough that there are miracles in life.**

expressions.en: We are all worms, but I do believe that I am a glow-worm.
expressions.zh: Churchill's quip. The author notes it would fail biology (glow-worms are mostly beetles or flies, not worms) but get an A in psychology.

expressions.en: the riot, the carnival, the salmagundi of worms
expressions.zh: A heaped-up list for the sheer exuberance of worms. *Salmagundi* is an old dish, a mixed salad of meats and vegetables, used figuratively for a jumble or medley.

expressions.en: the explosion had a long fuse
expressions.zh: The Cambrian "explosion" was not sudden: it had a long fuse burning through the ages before it.

expressions.en: a triskelion mounted on a pizza
expressions.zh: *Tribrachidium* looks like a three-legged triskelion symbol stuck on top of a pizza.

expressions.en: its insides have no inside
expressions.zh: A flatworm has no body cavity, so its insides have no inside: a neat paradox for a solid body.

expressions.en: with all the enthusiasm of teenagers on alcopops
expressions.zh: *Convoluta* gulps down algae with the eagerness of teenagers knocking back alcopops (sweet, fruit-flavoured alcoholic drinks).

expressions.en: Homo ergaster, the earliest member of the human genus, Adam had’em.
expressions.zh: A play on what is said to be the shortest poem in English, "Adam / Had 'em" (about fleas): tapeworms have been with us since the first members of our genus.

expressions.en: almost as bad as England in winter
expressions.zh: After the heat death of the universe everything is dark and cold, "almost as bad as England in winter": a self-mocking British aside.

expressions.en: the opposite of … ‘the heart of a heartless world’
expressions.zh: Marx called religion "the heart of a heartless world". The second law of thermodynamics is the reverse: a heartless core inside a world full of feeling.

expressions.en: He who kisses the joy as it flies, lives in eternity’s sun rise.
expressions.zh: From William Blake's "Eternity": whoever kisses joy as it flies, rather than trying to bind it to himself, lives in eternity's sunrise.

questions: The author says "appreciating" parasites can mean understanding rather than liking them. Is there something you dislike but appreciate in this sense?
Russell's "unyielding despair" or Čapek's becoming an earthworm to taste the soil: which attitude to death do you find more persuasive?
The name "flatworm" hides huge differences between two phyla. What other coarse labels like this exist in everyday language?

lede: The mantis shrimp, the size of a small cucumber, throws a punch as fast as a bullet, yet its eyes may be the most complex in the animal kingdom. From there the author explores the evolution of eyes, the bewildering variety of animal eyes, and how human "seeing" is really constructed by the brain.

points.body:
*Gonodactylus* means "genital finger"; the biologist who named it probably found its folded forelimbs funny. They are in fact raptorial appendages, and **a strike accelerates to nearly the speed of a bullet**, with a force of up to 1,500 newtons, perhaps the greatest in the animal kingdom relative to body weight. It is powered by a saddle-shaped (hyperbolic paraboloid) "spring" at the base of the limb, a structure also used in human architecture.

The strike is so fast that it creates cavitation bubbles in the water, and their collapse delivers **a second blow**. The roughly 400 species of stomatopods divide into "smashers" and "spearers", and the basic design has barely changed in more than four hundred million years.

points.h: The most complex eyes in the animal kingdom
points.body:
Each eye sits on a stalk that turns independently and has about ten thousand facets:
- Humans have three kinds of photoreceptor; mantis shrimps have **8 to 12**
- Each compound eye has three zones, each looking from a slightly different plane, like several sets of "trinocular" vision in one eye, giving very precise judgement of depth and distance
- They can see **circularly polarized light**, discovered only in 2008, which no other animal can; the gain in information is like stereo compared with mono

They also use their eyes for social life: territorial displays, ritualized fights, courtship, conveying mood and intent through postures and eye-like spots. Many people can accept a clever octopus but not a "thinking arthropod", yet stomatopods really are very cunning.

points.h: The world was blind for four-fifths of its history
points.body:
Galileo said the sun, with all those planets revolving around it, "can still ripen a bunch of grapes as if it had nothing else in the universe to do". Photosynthesis is at least 2.5 billion years old, but for about four-fifths of the history of life the world was blind; the first eyespots may have appeared less than 600 million years ago.

Getting from a light-sensitive spot to an image-forming eye seems to need a designer, but each small improvement in each generation is useful, and **it may take only 400,000 generations, under half a million years**. Put the mouse gene *Pax6*, which controls eye development, into a fruit-fly embryo and a fly eye grows where it was inserted: all eyes share a common genetic foundation.

- Trilobites: the earliest image-forming eyes in the fossil record, with calcite lenses
- *Opabinia*, the Cambrian animal with five stalked eyes and a pincer-like snout
- Corals track the moon with eyespots and release eggs and sperm together at full moon, an "upside-down snowstorm"
- Box jellyfish have 24 visual organs, three evolutionary stages in one body
- Giant clams have hundreds of pinhole eyes along the mantle
- The colossal squid's eyes are bigger than footballs
- The fiddler crab's periscope eyes; the deep-sea spookfish that focuses light with **mirrors** rather than lenses; dragonfish that emit red light their prey can't see, as "headlights"
- The barreleye's two tubular eyes sit inside a transparent, fluid-filled head, like two seats in a helicopter cockpit waiting for the pilots
- Proteins in migrating birds' eyes may use quantum effects to "see" Earth's magnetic field

points.h: Seeing is built by the brain
points.body:
"Seeing" and "knowing" share roots in language (Sanskrit *véda*, Latin *videre*). The eye is like a camera obscura, but who is looking at the image projected on the retina? Meister Eckhart said: "**We can only see the visible with the invisible.**"

Hold out your arm and raise your thumb: only a region narrower than your thumb is sharp, and 20 degrees off centre your vision is as poor as someone legally blind. We really have tunnel vision, compensated by **saccades** three times a second; during saccades the brain processes no information, so for a good part of the day we are effectively blind and the brain fills in by inference. The mantis shrimp's constantly swivelling eyes are an exaggerated version of what we do ourselves.

Gently press the skin below one open eye and the world shifts downward. The neuropsychologist Chris Frith says: **the brain embeds us in the world and then hides us.**

points.h: Learning to see, and being seen
points.body:
Babies are born with a preference for faces, eyes and "agents that move". Humans can also train remarkable vision: Moken children in the Andaman Sea deliberately constrict their pupils to see clearly underwater, and Swedish children have learned to do it too; sailors of old could see Venus in daylight.

Humans have more white of the eye than any other mammal, so others can tell from far away where we are looking: **we pass on information without speaking, and often give away our thoughts without meaning to**.

points.h: Golden birches by a Norwegian lake
points.body:
At seventeen, climbing alone in northern Norway, the author came across wild flowers glowing among black and grey stones, and thought that no one else would ever see these flowers or feel the wonder of this moment. Walking round a lake on the way down, sunlight broke through the clouds onto the birches and he felt **in resonance with all life**.

He does not share Schopenhauer's world-weariness, nor does he look to a god outside nature, but that experience taught him more about seeing, attention and presence. D. H. Lawrence said: "Thought is a man in his wholeness wholly attending."

The astrophysicist Jocelyn Bell Burnell says humans are all "electromagnetically challenged": we perceive only a narrow band of wavelengths. But with instruments we can see molecules and galaxies from the early universe, **becoming technological mantis shrimps covered in extra eyes**, like the angels "full of eyes round about" in Ezekiel's vision.

Mantis shrimp polarization vision may inspire new data storage devices. But where does all this lead? Without an inner vision, any number of instruments amount only to "blindsight". The chapter ends with Bashō: watching a bird fly until it vanishes over the sea and finds a small island.

expressions.en: It has the fastest genitals in the West
expressions.zh: The opening line parodies "the fastest gun in the West" from Westerns, because the animal's name means "genital finger".

expressions.en: diminutive marine Grendels
expressions.zh: Little Grendels of the sea. Grendel is the man-eating monster of *Beowulf*.

expressions.en: sunlight has driven a green fuse on Earth
expressions.zh: Echoing Dylan Thomas's line "The force that through the green fuse drives the flower": sunlight has lit a green fuse on Earth, driving all plant life.

expressions.en: an ‘upside-down snowstorm’ of semen and eggs
expressions.zh: Mass coral spawning, with eggs and sperm rising through the water, looks like a snowstorm falling upward.

expressions.en: as hard to imagine as a Zen koan
expressions.zh: What a box jellyfish sees is as hard to imagine as a Zen koan, a riddle meant to defeat ordinary reasoning.

expressions.en: couple in ways that would make fans of the Kama Sutra blush
expressions.zh: Their mating positions would make even devotees of the *Kama Sutra* blush.

expressions.en: Mostly it rained, except when it drizzled.
expressions.zh: Mostly it rained, except when it drizzled: classic British self-deprecation about the weather.

expressions.en: the brain embeds us in the world and then hides us
expressions.zh: The brain places us in the world, then hides itself: what we perceive is the brain's model, but we take it for the world itself.

expressions.en: we are all ‘electromagnetically challenged’
expressions.zh: A parody of euphemisms like "visually challenged": we are all "electromagnetically challenged", able to sense only a sliver of the spectrum.

expressions.en: What will be the inner vision without which all this is blindsight?
expressions.zh: *Blindsight* is the condition in which people with damage to the visual cortex respond to visual stimuli without being aware of seeing. The author asks what inner vision could keep all our instruments from being mere blindsight.

questions: Try the thumb experiment and the eyelid-pressing experiment. Knowing how many "gaps" and "fill-ins" your vision has, do you still believe that seeing is believing?
Mantis shrimps can see colours and polarized light we cannot imagine. Do you think "seeing more" necessarily means "understanding more"?
The author's experience by the Norwegian lake contrasts with the "technological mantis shrimp". In an age of ubiquitous instruments, what is the value of unmediated seeing?

lede: What makes humans human? The author starts with an unremarkable pair of feet: without walking on two legs there would be no big brain and no language, and without something like music, language would never have appeared. He ends with the story of Orpheus and the question of when to look back.

points.body:
In most primates the hind limbs are grasping hands, but ours have become two "arched pads of meat, with a round chin at one end and a stubby thumb tied to the little fingers". Watching a possum tap tree bark with its fingers to find grubs, the zoologist Jonathan Kingdon guessed that the dexterous hand might be a 140-million-year-old inheritance.

Feet look useless, but look at them another way: the comedian Billy Connolly said Scotland's contribution to world history was *staggering*, and it is feet that make staggering possible. Humans can walk long distances effortlessly and, in the right conditions, can run the fastest four-legged animals into exhaustion.

Plato defined man as a "featherless biped"; Diogenes brought in a plucked chicken: "Here is Plato's man." Plato added "with broad nails".

Humans have also been defined as the political animal, the laughing animal, the tool-making, religious, cooking and storytelling animal, the only animal that likes hot sauce. As one poet puts it, **humans seem to be the only animal anxious about what makes it unique.** Tools, theory of mind, culture and morality have all been found in other animals; Michael Gazzaniga suggests human uniqueness may lie in **inhibiting impulses and delaying gratification**.

points.h: A short history of walking on two legs
points.body:
The first bipedal land animals were early dinosaurs about 230 million years ago, such as *Eoraptor*, the "dawn hunter from the Valley of the Moon". Today the basilisk lizard can run across water like a "super-charged Charlie Chaplin", earning the name "Jesus lizard". The most successful flightless bird is the chicken, a relative of *Tyrannosaurus*; there are more than twenty billion on Earth at any time, but only through human enslavement and modification. The kangaroo, meanwhile, is a "marsupial pogo stick".

The Laetoli footprints of 3.7 million years ago show that "Lucy" already walked upright as we do, though with long arms, short legs and a brain a third the size of ours. *Homo habilis* was better adapted to life on the ground but still often ended up as lunch for sabre-toothed cats.

The endurance running hypothesis: early humans ran long distances in the heat of the savannah sun, chasing four-legged animals to exhaustion or getting first to carcasses left in the sun by other predators. There are some 26 lines of evidence:
- The big tendons in the legs act like springs, more than doubling efficiency
- Sweat glands all over the body shed heat
- The gluteus maximus is so "maximus" to keep us balanced while running
- Short toes, and a nuchal ligament that steadies the head

Running brings *Funktionslust*: the pleasure of doing what you were made to do. For more than 99 per cent of human history, continual movement was the norm.

points.h: Language came from something like music
points.body:
Language lets us make endless propositions, but why did it arise? Evolutionary psychologists say humans first developed "deep intersubjectivity": mind-reading, empathy and sympathy. The archaeologist Steven Mithen proposes a communication system called **Hmmmmm**: holistic, manipulative, multi-modal, musical and mimetic. It was neither music nor language but something music-like, which split into music and language only about a hundred thousand years ago.

Steven Pinker calls music "auditory cheesecake", a by-product of evolution; Darwin saw music as sexual display like the peacock's tail: "the rock star always gets the girl (or boy)". The author thinks neither is the whole story: **music and dance let people move in sync and form bonds**, regulate emotion; a mother's songs and a baby's babbling are the first emotional channel, and music can even help patients recover speech and movement.

When fully upright, the spinal cord enters the skull from directly below, the larynx sits lower and the vocal tract is longer, so we can make a wider range of sounds. Bipedalism also freed the fixed link between stride and breath: an ape's torso takes the strain of walking, so it cannot walk and vocalize at once, but **humans can walk and talk, even walk and chew gum**; when running we can choose different stride-to-breath ratios. The result: rhythm, song, language, and the distinctively human laugh. The poet George Seferis said: "Poetry has its roots in human breath."

The Babenzele Pygmies of the Congo combine polyphony with polyrhythm (eight, three, nine and twelve beats layered together), which Westerners at first find hard to follow. The anthropologist Jerome Lewis suggests first listening to the forest they live in: monkeys and birds call at different times, and together they make the sound of the forest. For the Babenzele these are "**technologies of enchantment**": when the voices interlock just right, people forget themselves and enter a calm ecstasy.

Aristotle asked why rhythms and melodies, which are only sounds, resemble states of the soul. The author's answer: music combines heartbeat, breath, stride and attention to the world outside us, **making the individual more vivid while letting them merge, for a time, into something larger**.

Orpheus's music enchanted birds and beasts and made trees and stones dance, yet as he left the underworld he looked back and lost Eurydice for ever. The author ventures three readings:
- **The power of music** is so great it seems to overcome death; whale song, like the photographs of Earth from space, punctures human self-centredness
- **Restraint**: at the crucial moment he could not control his impulse. Odysseus managed not to eat the cattle of the sun god, but could not stop his companions
- Not "never look back", but **knowing when and how to look back**. Nietzsche's eternal recurrence means embracing everything that made us, including our evolutionary origins and our kinship with other animals

Jared Diamond says humans forty thousand years ago were "just another species of big mammal". The author finds this unimaginative and prefers the sculptor Emily Young's picture: for hundreds of thousands of years people sat under trees knapping flint, and those rhythms, mingled with cicadas and birdsong, **were music in themselves**.

expressions.en: they have jelly on them
expressions.zh: Human hands can build whole worlds, even when, like the hands of Linus in *Peanuts*, they have jelly on them.

expressions.en: ‘plates of meat’ (as Cockney rhyming slang has it)
expressions.zh: Cockney rhyming slang: *plates of meat* rhymes with *feet*, so it means feet.

expressions.en: Scotland’s contribution to world history was staggering
expressions.zh: Billy Connolly's pun: *staggering* means both astonishing and lurching drunkenly.

expressions.en: a frabjous bird
expressions.zh: *Frabjous* is Lewis Carroll's coinage in "Jabberwocky" ("O frabjous day!"), probably a blend of *fabulous* and *joyous*, here applied to the blue-footed booby.

expressions.en: Moving like a super-charged Charlie Chaplin
expressions.zh: The basilisk lizard sprinting across water like a turbocharged Charlie Chaplin, all flailing legs and speed.

expressions.en: a kangaroo is a marsupial pogo stick
expressions.zh: The kangaroo as a marsupial pogo stick: a bouncing spring-loaded toy with a pouch.

expressions.en: Each gluteus on our bottom is so maximus because this helps us to run well
expressions.zh: A joke that splits the anatomical name *gluteus maximus* (the main buttock muscle): each buttock is so "maximus" because big glutes help us run.

expressions.en: auditory cheesecake
expressions.zh: Steven Pinker's famous phrase: music as "auditory cheesecake", delicious but not something evolution needed.

expressions.en: technologies of enchantment
expressions.zh: Lewis's phrase for Babenzele polyphony: a technique for producing enchantment, letting people lose themselves in a larger group.

expressions.en: an erect, musical, featherless running biped . . . sometimes given to staggering
expressions.zh: The author's new definition of a human: an upright, musical, featherless running biped... occasionally given to staggering, in both of Connolly's senses.

questions: For a musician with a jazz piano background: do you find Mithen's "Hmmmmm" hypothesis (that music and language share an origin) convincing? Have you ever felt something like "communication" while playing?
Pinker says music is "auditory cheesecake". How would you argue against that?
"Knowing when and how to look back": for a creator, when is looking back at your own past work or a tradition helpful, and when is it a trap?

lede: More than a thousand metres down, a sea fan's trunk spirals like a corkscrew with feathery branches at even intervals, looking more like a mathematical theorem than an animal. From there the author turns to symmetry, spirals, the DNA double helix, viruses, and what beauty really is.

points.body:
*Iridogorgia* is a gorgonian (sea fan), a distant relative of jellyfish and stony corals, but its polyps have **eight-fold symmetry** (stony corals have six). It lives a mile down; brought up into the light it shimmers with iridescence, and in 1883 someone compared it to burnished gold, mother-of-pearl and the most brilliant tropical beetles.

Most striking is the symmetry: **an elegant spiral trunk with regularly spaced, feathery branches.** It leaves an afterimage, and the author thinks it resembles two twentieth-century artefacts: Duchamp's 1914 readymade *Bottle Rack*, and Watson and Crick's model of DNA. The first sought to go beyond "retinal art" and reach the viewer's mind directly; the second sought to understand the "code" behind visible life.

points.h: From Platonic solids to the symmetry of the Big Bang
points.body:
Plato held that the five regular polyhedra were beauty itself and the basis of existence. Kepler used nested regular polyhedra to explain the planetary orbits; as recently as 2003 cosmologists proposed that the universe might be a finite dodecahedron. The physicist Michio Kaku says the beauty and symmetry of shells, ice crystals, galaxies and even subatomic particles **are all fragments of the original symmetry that broke at the moment of the Big Bang**.

Until the mid-eighteenth century many people thought crystals, which assemble themselves, were alive; Linnaeus put them in a fourth "kingdom".

Radiolarians are single-celled plankton older than multicellular life. In *Art Forms in Nature*, Ernst Haeckel drew them as geodesic domes, buckyballs, exuberant Samurai helmets and *Jugendstil* lampshades; he believed in an almost mystical creative force in nature.

D'Arcy Thompson was more empirical: behind form lie simple physical forces, like soap film forming bubbles on a wire frame. In *On Growth and Form* (1917) he drew the outlines of organisms on squared paper and stretched the grid, turning one species into another. Stephen Jay Gould called him **a hybrid of Pythagoras and Newton**.

From sunflower florets and elephant trunks to the path of a moth around a flame, spirals are everywhere; mollusc shells grow into equiangular spirals at every angle. Thompson said these shells follow laws so simple and harmonious that "**none is better than another, none more or less fitted to survive**": nature is not cruel competition but endless creation, counterpoint and fugue.

From cave paintings twenty thousand years old to the triple spiral at Newgrange and the spiral minaret of Samarra, humans have always been drawn to spirals. Perhaps because a spiral is **a constant shape within flow**, as in Carl Woese's image of life: "resilient patterns in a turbulent flow".

points.h: DNA: older than the hills, and for ever young
points.body:
Thompson admitted his book "only takes us to the threshold". The discovery of the DNA double helix in 1953 opened the next door: all life unfolds from the geometry of an "aperiodic crystal".
- It is older than virtually all of the hills: the common ancestor that used it lived at least 3.5 billion years ago
- The DNA in one cell, stretched out, is nearly two metres long; the DNA in one human body could reach to the sun and back hundreds of times; the DNA of a few thousand people would reach the nearest star
- Changing 1 per cent of the non-coding region of a human-sized genome gives more possible combinations than the number of grains of sand that would fill the universe

The Nobel laureate George Wald joked: **if a genome wants to swim in the sea, it makes itself a fish; if it wants to go to Harvard, it makes itself a man.**

Francis Crick's "central dogma" held that information flows only from DNA to protein. In *The Selfish Gene* Richard Dawkins wrote that genes sit safe inside "gigantic lumbering robots", manipulating the world by remote control.

The physiologist Denis Noble sees this as a rhetorical trick, and offers an equally valid rewrite: genes are "**trapped** inside highly intelligent beings, moulded by the outside world... it is we who allow their code to be read". Today the genome looks far from a complete map of life: epigenetics shows that cells read DNA more like **interpreting a script** than running a program, and less than 2 per cent of DNA codes for proteins.

At least 8 per cent of the human genome comes from endogenous retroviruses. The bad side: viruses can devastate their hosts, and engineered viruses could bring unprecedented catastrophe. The good side:
- Viruses evolve a million times faster than their hosts, and there are more viruses on Earth than stars in the universe
- About a hundred million tonnes of microbes are killed by viruses in the ocean every minute, and as they burst they feed new life: **viruses create new life by fomenting death**
- Key genes for forming the placenta come from viruses: "without viruses, human beings would still be laying eggs"
- They also took part in the evolution of the immune system and gene regulatory networks

Viruses show us that we are products of different things interacting, like the Buddhist idea of "dependent origination".
