Life is information, and also matter (65 per cent oxygen, 18 per cent carbon...); but Chopin's late works are more than marks on paper and vibrations in the air, and **a dancer is more than DNA**.

Evolutionary psychology offers four layers of explanation: in art we see the good qualities of a mate; natural patterns suggest a skilled "creator"; aesthetic "good form" corresponds to evolutionarily "stable form"; and the "attractor states" of non-living systems (snowflakes, phases of the moon) are taken as evidence of gods. The author finds this insufficient: beauty is also shaped by history, and these explanations miss **the experience of beauty**, which lets us see that things exist independently of our feelings and compels our full attention.

In the food-poor deep sea, *Iridogorgia* makes itself into a net, like a spider's web hung with dew; three new species of *Iridogorgia* were found in 2007 alone. These new worlds are being destroyed by humans faster than anyone expected, which gives us a new responsibility, and the possibility of what Spinoza called "beautiful action".

Martin Rees notes that medieval Europeans thought the universe small and short-lived, yet still dreamed on a grand scale, spending their lives building cathedrals they would never see finished. **Today we know so much more: what might we conceive?**

expressions.en: more like something from a mathematical theorem than the animal kingdom
expressions.zh: It looks more like something out of a mathematical theorem than out of the animal kingdom: a measure of how perfect its geometry is.

expressions.en: Looking at this gorgon … won’t turn you to stone
expressions.zh: *Gorgonian* sea fans are named after the Gorgon, the snake-haired monster whose gaze turned people to stone. Looking at this one won't petrify you, the author says, but it may leave an afterimage.

expressions.en: exuberant Samurai helmets and Jugendstil lampshades
expressions.zh: Haeckel's radiolarians look like flamboyant Samurai helmets and *Jugendstil* (German Art Nouveau) lampshades.

expressions.en: a hybrid of Pythagoras and Newton
expressions.zh: Gould's description of D'Arcy Thompson's thinking: part Pythagoras (number and harmony), part Newton (physical force).

expressions.en: organisms [as] resilient patterns in a turbulent flow
expressions.zh: Carl Woese's image of life: organisms are not things but durable patterns in a turbulent flow, like a whirlpool that persists while the water moves through it.

expressions.en: DNA is older than virtually all of the hills
expressions.zh: A twist on the idiom "as old as the hills" (extremely old): DNA is older than almost every hill on Earth.

expressions.en: from lampreys to Lady Gaga
expressions.zh: From lampreys to Lady Gaga: another absurdly wide, alliterative span covering the range of life DNA has produced.

expressions.en: If it wants to go to Harvard, it makes itself a man.
expressions.zh: George Wald's joke: the genome builds whatever body suits its ambitions, a fish for the sea or a human to attend Harvard.

expressions.en: without viruses, human beings would still be laying eggs
expressions.zh: Without viruses humans would still be laying eggs, because key placental genes came from viruses.

expressions.en: viruses create new life by fomenting death
expressions.zh: Viruses bring about new life by stirring up death. To *foment* is to incite or stir up trouble.

expressions.en: A dancer is more than DNA.
expressions.zh: A dancer is more than DNA: the living whole is not reducible to its code.

expressions.en: ‘biology speaks the language of courtier and troubadour’
expressions.zh: In butterfly wings, the dances of grebes and the song of the nightingale, "biology speaks the language of courtier and troubadour": the language of courtship, display and love song.

questions: Dawkins and Noble describe the same facts in two ways. Which do you prefer? Is it only a difference of rhetoric?
Thompson says that among shell forms "none is more fitted to survive". Does that contradict "survival of the fittest"?
As a creator working in both music and visuals, do you think evolutionary psychology's explanations of beauty can account for the kind of beauty you pursue in your work? What is missing?

lede: Japanese macaques soaking in hot springs in the snow look like Zen monks in meditation, but only high-ranking monkeys get into the pool while the rest shiver nearby. This chapter asks: is human nature Machiavellian scheming, or cooperation and sympathy?

points.body:
The Japanese macaque is the only primate apart from humans adapted to such a cold climate, and humans bring clothes and fire. (Bathing in hot springs began only after the Second World War with human encouragement, and only a few troops do it.) The macaque genus was once the most widespread and successful primate on Earth.

Space in the pool is limited and the rules are brutal: the ruling family is led by an adult female, paired with a male who enforces order and is driven out when he grows old or weak; other families form alliances to stage coups. **Snow monkeys are sometimes more like yakuza than monks.**

The primatologist Dario Maestripieri says macaques are the model of Machiavellian intelligence: like them, humans succeed through their most calculating and ruthless side. He jokes that when humans start the nuclear war that ends civilization there will be no gorillas left, so Earth won't become a *Planet of the Apes*, **but there will probably still be plenty of rhesus macaques.**

These behaviours are real, but using them to support "veneer theory" (people seem kind but at heart care only for themselves) gives a complete picture neither of monkeys nor of humans, and is no basis for imagining our future.

Indians hold macaques sacred because of Hanuman; ancient Japan built shrines to snow monkeys; the Chinese treasured the song of the gibbon, but both China and Japan also painted "monkeys grasping at the moon's reflection" to mock human folly. Europeans swung between humanizing apes and bestializing humans: in the Middle Ages the ape was an image of the devil, and Shakespeare used the ape for "proud man, dressed in a little brief authority".

For a century after their discovery, gorillas were portrayed as savage subhuman monsters, the exact opposite of the nature of these gentle vegetarians.

Darwin's notebook, 1838: "**He who understands baboon would do more towards metaphysics than Locke.**"

But his "struggle for existence" was selectively amplified:
- T. H. Huxley saw humans as "cleverer brutes" who could only hold down their animal nature by reason; civilization was a thin crust
- Freud traced morality to the sons' collective murder of the father
- The Soviet scientist Ilya Ivanov inseminated chimpanzees with human sperm in an attempt to make "humanzees"
- Rockefeller said the victory of big corporations was "a law of nature and a law of God"; Gordon Gekko in *Wall Street*: **greed is good**
- In Cold War game theory every player was a ruthless self-maximizer
- Enron, inspired by *The Selfish Gene*, adopted "rank and yank", creating a ruthless and dishonest corporate culture that collapsed in 2001

points.h: The opposite error: the blank slate
points.body:
Orwell's O'Brien says: "We create human nature. Men are infinitely malleable." Mao said the Chinese people were "a blank sheet of paper", and in the Great Leap Forward between twenty or thirty million and more than forty million people starved. B. F. Skinner insisted that all mental activity was "explanatory fiction".

In the late 1960s two American psychologists built a series of "monster mothers" for newborn rhesus monkeys: they blasted high-pressure air, shook violently, catapulted the infants off, or pushed out brass spikes. **Each time, the infant waited until it stopped, then climbed back and clung tighter.** Only total isolation from birth could drive the monkeys mad.

points.h: The Darwin of *The Descent of Man*
points.body:
Darwin later went further: any animal with well-marked social instincts, once its intellect developed to near the human level, **would inevitably acquire a moral sense or conscience**. He quoted an account from Abyssinia: a large male baboon walked down the hill alone and led a six-month-old baboon away from a pack of dogs, "the dogs being too much astonished to attack".

Today the evidence is abundant. Mozu, a Japanese macaque born without hands or feet, was fed and protected by her troop, lived long and raised five offspring; laboratory rhesus monkeys that saw that pulling a lever made another monkey suffer kept refusing to pull it for a reward. Ahla, a baboon on a South African farm, could return more than twenty identical lambs accurately to their own mothers. **Mirror neurons** were first discovered in the brains of rhesus macaques.

Adam Smith wrote that however selfish a man may be, there are principles in his nature that make him interested in the fortune of others. But whether sympathy shows depends on the situation: in Milgram's experiment about two-thirds of ordinary people, ordered by authority, were willing to give what they believed were lethal shocks.

Frans de Waal says biology "holds us on a leash". We have two inner apes: one that **reinforces hierarchy** and one that **undermines it**. The author adds that institutions differ from individuals: communities can consciously build institutions in which the cooperative side prevails. Perhaps *The Prince* is satire, "the *1984* of 1513", and Machiavelli's true convictions are in the *Discourses on Livy*: a republic of free debate is better than tyranny.

Steven Pinker says humans are becoming less violent; the mathematical biologist Martin Nowak thinks Kropotkin was right that **mutual aid is a factor of evolution**: cooperation (the "snuggle for existence") is a third pillar alongside mutation and natural selection. What matters is the relative rate at which cooperators meet cooperators and defectors form gangs, and that is something we can influence.

The Dalai Lama asked Elie Wiesel what had helped the Jewish people. The answer: a book, solidarity and memory. The author says the best such book is "the book of life", in which our common origins are plain to see. Chekhov: **show man what he is like, and he will become better.**

points.h: They would fit in a stadium
points.body:
About half of the 634 living species of monkeys, apes and lemurs are endangered; all the individuals of the 25 most endangered species would not fill a football stadium. Orangutans in Indonesia's rainforests are being burned to death in large numbers. Watching an orangutan mother and child in a zoo, John Berger was reminded of Cosimo Tura's *Madonna and Child*: that protectiveness and tenderness have lasted millions of years.

The ending: science demands radical honesty, a constant search for ways not to deceive ourselves, and so it stands on the side of "the better angels of our nature". **Or else we are no wise monkeys.**

expressions.en: We are monkeys with guns and money.
expressions.zh: The chapter's epigraph, from Tom Waits: we are monkeys with guns and money.

expressions.en: eyes that are close-set like those of George W. Bush
expressions.zh: Close-set eyes like George W. Bush's: a passing political jab.

expressions.en: gets first dibs for the choicest spots
expressions.zh: *First dibs* is informal for the first claim or first choice of something.

expressions.en: enough manipulation and machination to make a Borgia blush
expressions.zh: Enough plotting and scheming to make a Borgia blush. The Borgias were a Renaissance family notorious for intrigue and poisoning.

expressions.en: tumescent with internationalism
expressions.zh: The young Castro "tumescent with internationalism": *tumescent* means swollen, often with a sexual sense, which makes the phrase mocking.

expressions.en: ‘Civilization is intermittent.’
expressions.zh: Menachem Begin's line: civilization is intermittent, not a permanent state but something that switches on and off.

expressions.en: The Prince is the 1984 of 1513
expressions.zh: *The Prince* as the *1984* of 1513: read not as a manual for tyrants but as a satire exposing them, as Orwell's novel exposes totalitarianism.

expressions.en: the snuggle for existence
expressions.zh: Nowak's one-letter change to Darwin's "struggle for existence": cooperation, the snuggle for existence, matters as much as competition.

expressions.en: make me one with everything
expressions.zh: The joke: the Dalai Lama walks into a pizza shop and says "Make me one with everything", meaning both "one pizza with all toppings" and "unite me with all things". The author says he didn't get the joke, but is "a wily old fox".

expressions.en: Or else we are no wise monkeys.
expressions.zh: Echoing the Japanese "three wise monkeys" (see no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil): unless we stay honest with ourselves, we will not be wise monkeys at all.

questions: Ideas like "greed is good" and "rank and yank" are often self-fulfilling. Have you seen systems at work or in life where a prophecy fulfilled itself?
De Waal's two inner apes: one reinforcing hierarchy, one undermining it. Which do you think is stronger in you? In what situations do you switch?
The "monster mother" experiments on rhesus monkeys produced important findings, but by extremely cruel means. Does science have the right to do this?

lede: The fierce, fearless honey badger, and a little bird, the honeyguide, that leads people to bees' nests. From rumours of "man-eating badgers" in Basra to the whistles of Tanzania's Hadza, the author speculates that human language may have grown partly out of cooperation with other animals.

points.body:
In the summer of 2007, Basra under British occupation was racked by violence. Rumours spread of a monster with a monkey's head and a dog's body that tore apart live cattle at night, broke into homes and could not be stopped by bullets; some said the British had released trained badgers to take revenge on civilians. A British spokesman said, with a straight face: "We can categorically state that we have not released man-eating badgers into the area."

The rumour had a grain of truth: the honey badger is only the size of a small dog but fierce and fearless, the pit bull of the badger world, only more agile and more robust. More likely the war had driven them out of the scrub and marshes beyond the city.

Herodotus wrote of a fierce animal in the Indian desert, bigger than a fox and smaller than a dog, that dug up gold from the sand; those who stole the gold had to flee on the fastest camels. If the story has a basis in reality it was probably the honey badger, and the "gold" may have been the honey it digs out.

- It can drive lions away from a wildebeest carcass
- The skin on its throat is thick and loose against bites from its own kind, so rivals go for the testicles instead, making the other bleed to death
- It hardly fears highly venomous snakes, shrugs off bee stings, and can stupefy a swarm with a foul spray from glands near its anus

The author hopes this "ornery hellion" will be one of the few medium-sized mammals that can survive the worst of human impact without needing protectors. **It is good to have a companion animal that is not under our control and has more charisma than cockroaches and super-rats.**

points.h: The honeyguide: a bird that shows the way
points.body:
The honeyguide's scientific name is *Indicator indicator* (really). It loves beeswax but is too small to open a nest and fears stings, so it gets badgers and humans to do the work. It perches nearby and calls repeatedly; once it has attention it flies toward the nest in stages, flashing its pale tail feathers, and comes back if its follower gets lost. At the nest it changes its call and waits patiently. The honey goes to the helper, the wax to the bird.

Humans have gone further: the Boran people of Kenya and Ethiopia summon it with a whistle, *fuulido*, audible a kilometre away, cutting the average time to find a nest from nine hours to three. Rock art shows this cooperation is at least two thousand years old.

points.h: The Hadza and the oldest names
points.body:
The language of Tanzania's Hadza may be one of the oldest still spoken. They call the honey badger *Kìrìphá-kò* and the honeyguide *Thìk’ìlí-ko*, and the two words may be related. Their ancestors may have lived in the same place for fifty thousand years as hunter-gatherers, without farming, herding or permanent dwellings.

The author admits he can't pronounce the clicks well but wants to try, out of respect for the Hadza. They are tough enough to have resisted forced settlement by both the colonial government and the Tanzanian state, and gentle with one another, with men and women sharing childcare more than in most societies. Fewer than a thousand still live the traditional way.

The relationship between the Hadza and the honeyguide is not domestication but **a partnership of near-equals**, what the poet Muir called "an old, lost companionship". They celebrate a successful day with a kind of "traditional drama": one man whistles and plays the bird, another plays the man following it and imitating its calls.

The author speculates that language is rooted partly in **paying attention to the calls and traces of other creatures**, and became more reflective and richer through retelling and celebrating them. Variants of the FOXP2 gene and the archaeological record of "behavioural modernity" show that language emerged along a path of its own, but it did not happen in a vacuum. David Abram says: "**We are human only in contact, and conviviality, with what is not human.**"

Thoreau honed language into a tool for pure attention; shortly before he died he was still noting in his journal how rain falling on stones showed the direction of the wind. But Wang Wei says we easily "roam the delusion of words"; there is always a gap between the richness of experience and the narrow, linear bandwidth of language. Our language and our cognitive maps may still be like the German globe of 1492 that has **no America** on it.

In tenth-century Basra, a Sufi brotherhood wrote *The Case of the Animals versus Man*: the animals bring their complaint before the court of the King of the Jinn, which rules that humans have no right to enslave and destroy them.

points.h: Paying attention to birds is paying attention to life
points.body: Some important things can be fully experienced only when we do not rely entirely on symbols, birdsong for example. The writer Graeme Gibson says our species became self-aware surrounded by birds. **We need the honey badger's toughness and the honeyguide's ingenuity to survive**, and both deserve celebration and respect.

expressions.en: Cet animal est très méchant. Quand on l’attaque il se defend.
expressions.zh: The chapter's epigraph, a French saying: "This animal is very wicked: when attacked, it defends itself." It mocks human double standards.

expressions.en: We don’t need no stinking badgers.
expressions.zh: An online joke at the British statement, adapting the famous line from *The Treasure of the Sierra Madre*, "We don't need no stinking badges", with *badges* turned into *badgers*.

expressions.en: recruited by perfidious Albion
expressions.zh: *Perfidious Albion* (treacherous England) is an old continental insult for Britain, here mocking the idea that the badgers were British agents.

expressions.en: find the video ‘The Crazy Nastyass Honey Badger’ on the web
expressions.zh: "For a less academic account, find 'The Crazy Nastyass Honey Badger' online": a narrated video that went viral in 2011, famous for the line "Honey badger don't care".

expressions.en: this ornery hellion
expressions.zh: *Ornery* is American slang for bad-tempered and stubborn; a *hellion* is a troublemaker or little devil.

expressions.en: Indicator indicator (yes, really)
expressions.zh: The scientific name repeats itself, "Indicator indicator", and the author adds that yes, this is real.

expressions.en: gambling with poisoned arrows
expressions.zh: Hadza men's leisure consists mainly of sitting around gambling with poisoned arrows as stakes.

expressions.en: humanity evolved in commun(icat)ion with other animals
expressions.zh: The bracket splits the word so it reads two ways: humanity evolved in *communion* with other animals and in *communication* with them.

expressions.en: ‘roam the delusion of words’
expressions.zh: Wang Wei's phrase: to wander in the illusions created by words, mistaking language for reality.

questions: The relationship between humans and honeyguides is neither domestication nor predation but near-equal cooperation. Do relationships like this between humans and animals still exist today?
The author thinks language came partly from paying attention to other creatures. In your music or visual work, have you ever found a "language" in natural sounds or animal behaviour?
What would humanity lose if cultures like the Hadza's disappear? Only languages and knowledge?

lede: One night in West Papua the author touched a leatherback turtle as she laid her eggs, and she was warm. This turtle, a contemporary of the dinosaurs, has barely changed since, yet in a few decades its numbers have fallen by nine-tenths. Beyond pessimism, the author looks for what can be done, and also takes the turtle as an object of meditation on existence itself.

points.body:
The leatherback spends more than 99 per cent of its life at sea and swims fast and powerfully, but on land its half-tonne body becomes "a cruel joke". The female levers herself up the beach bit by bit with her huge front flippers, like carrying a heavy pack on a 5,500-metre plateau, where every step feels like hauling a grand piano.

She digs a shallow pit with her front flippers, then enters a trance and, with her far more dexterous rear flippers, digs **entirely by touch** a narrow-necked, jar-shaped egg chamber, patting the walls firm with the precision of a master potter. She lays dozens of ping-pong-ball eggs, fills in the sand and scatters it about to hide the spot. The author recalls Zhuangzi: all things under heaven have dimensions beyond measure.

- Its front flippers, like a humpback whale's, are disproportionately large
- Its shell is shaped like a teardrop or almond, with seven ridges running lengthwise like the ribs on the back of a lute, and it feels like the firm foam of a computer mouse mat
- Its throat is lined with backward-pointing spines designed for jellyfish
- The thick "tears" running from its slanting eyes are really excreting salt

A group of people from rich countries cheered like children. Afterwards the author reflected: we see ourselves as "good people", yet we are beneficiaries of the civilization that is destroying these animals; **it is too easy to push responsibility for the destruction onto others.**

points.h: Creatures that went back to the sea
points.body:
Werner Herzog called the ocean a "merciless hell", from which some species escaped onto land. The author thinks this says more about the director: for over 200 million years land animals have been returning to the sea and evolving astonishing forms there.

Turtles were among the earliest and most persistent returners: *Odontochelys*, about 220 million years old, had a belly plate but no upper shell; the Cretaceous *Archelon* was more than four metres across, bigger than the turret of a main battle tank. The leatherback evolved between 110 and 90 million years ago and has barely changed since: **while *Tyrannosaurus* lurked in the forests, leatherbacks were laying eggs on the same beaches.**

points.h: A super-traveller that lives on jellyfish
points.body:
They survived the mass extinction that killed the dinosaurs, probably thanks to their streamlined shape and undemanding diet:
- The ridges on the back act like keels, stabilizing the body and increasing speed
- A leatherback can eat its own body weight in jellyfish in a day; one ate 69 tyre-sized lion's mane jellyfish in three hours
- It generates heat to keep warm, swimming further and into colder water than other reptiles; the largest individuals have turned up off the coast of Wales
- It may dive deeper than any animal except the sperm whale
- It senses Earth's magnetic field; only in 2006 was it found that some swim from South-East Asia to North America and back

Small changes in incubation temperature decide the sex of the hatchlings.

Drowned in fishing gear, choked by plastic bags, hit by ships, slaughtered for meat, eggs dug up for food or aphrodisiacs. By 2000 the data showed a 90 per cent fall over twenty years.

Off southern Cuba, Columbus saw "the sea full of turtles... so many that the ships seemed about to run aground on them"; a 1774 *History of Jamaica* said ships that lost their way could find the Cayman Islands **by following the sound of turtles swimming**. Today it is rare to see even one in those waters. On Mexico's Pacific coast some 75,000 females nested in the early 1980s; now only a few hundred remain.

points.h: Can we help bring about recovery?
points.body:
It is not hopeless everywhere: on St Croix in the Caribbean, nesting females increased from about 20 in 1980 to 200 in 2000, and hatchlings from 2,000 to fifty thousand.

The marine biologist Carl Safina says the question he asks is no longer "what are the problems?" but "**can we help bring about recovery?**" The answer is yes: local people protecting nests on the beach buys time to tackle the longer-term problems (twenty billion longline hooks a year in the Pacific, plastic, warming that makes the sand too hot). "The way you avoid despair is to focus on what works and what you can do, grab hold of it, and don't let go."

"The world rests on a turtle's back. What's under the turtle? It's turtles all the way down." The author says that as a metaphor this is not absurd: the matter we can see is only a small part of the universe, and if there is a multiverse, then in a sense it really is turtles all the way down.

He compares the leatherback to a Japanese dry garden: some see only twigs, stones and gravel, others see mountains in clouds and islands in the sea; the objects are still, and the movement happens in the mind. A leatherback coming towards you underwater is like a great boulder that captures your attention and then quickly melts into the blue, **like consciousness itself**. With a brain no bigger than a grape, in its unknowing it performs a kind of grace.

The sky cleared, the starlight bright enough to cast shadows, and a nest of hatchlings laid weeks earlier broke out of their shells and raced for the sea like tiny rugby players going for the touchline, the pearly spots on their backs arranged in teardrop shapes.

The great majority will be eaten, and most survivors will probably be ground up in the mincing machine of human civilization. But perhaps a few will live, grow to two thousand times their weight at departure, and once again haul "the boulder of their own existence" up the sand. Camus said: **one must imagine Sisyphus happy.** Somewhere among countless universes, perhaps the gods are smiling.

expressions.en: their own mass … becomes a cruel joke
expressions.zh: On land, the turtle's own weight, so effortless at sea, becomes a cruel joke played on it.

expressions.en: every step was like hauling a grand piano
expressions.zh: Carrying a heavy pack at high altitude, every step felt like dragging a grand piano: the author's image for the female turtle's struggle up the beach.

expressions.en: jellyfish are bread and butter to a Leatherback
expressions.zh: *Bread and butter* means everyday staple food or basic livelihood: jellyfish are the leatherback's daily fare.

expressions.en: Pangea – the original turtle island
expressions.zh: Pangaea as the original "turtle island", alluding to the name Turtle Island used by many Native North American peoples for the continent.

expressions.en: the living bouillabaisse of the Cretaceous ocean
expressions.zh: The Cretaceous ocean as a living bouillabaisse, the Marseille fish stew: a teeming broth of creatures.

expressions.en: To list the many ways they die is to despair
expressions.zh: Listing all the ways they die is enough to drive one to despair.

expressions.en: turtles all the way down
expressions.zh: "Turtles all the way down": the punchline of a famous anecdote about a world resting on a turtle standing on another turtle, used for any infinite regress.

expressions.en: a ‘gateless gate’
expressions.zh: The Zen "gateless gate" (*Mumonkan*): the dry garden is a gate without a gate, an entrance only the mind can pass through.

expressions.en: determined as tiny rugby players going for a touchline
expressions.zh: The hatchlings dash for the sea as single-mindedly as small rugby players racing for the touchline.

expressions.en: going like the blazes
expressions.zh: *Going like the blazes* is an informal phrase for going flat out, as fast as possible.

expressions.en: one must imagine Sisyphus happy
expressions.zh: The closing line of Camus's *The Myth of Sisyphus*: meaning is found in the struggle itself, even an endless one.

questions: The author admits he is a "beneficiary of the civilization that is destroying these animals". As an individual, what is the most honest response to that situation?
Safina says the way to avoid despair is to focus on what you can do. Is that an effective mindset, or a form of self-consolation?
The leatherback has a brain the size of a grape, yet "performs a kind of grace in its unknowing". Is there a difference between beauty without consciousness and beauty with it?

lede: The bearded jumping spider has a white beard and black tufts, and two pairs of front eyes. Look at it and your gaze jumps back and forth between the pairs, unable to settle, as in the duck-rabbit illusion. A tiny jumping spider opens up reflections on attention, memory and forgetting.

points.body: Someone in Yorkshire saw a message from God in Arabic inside a tomato. Either the Almighty likes to reveal himself in fruit and vegetables, or this is **apophenia**: seeing meaning where there is none. We all see faces in inanimate things (*pareidolia*); evolutionary psychology explains that mistaking a rock in the grass for a lion's face costs far less than the opposite mistake.

points.h: A face you can't focus on
points.body: The bearded jumping spider has a face, with snow-white whiskers around the mouth and pointed black tufts on top, but **its anterior median and anterior lateral eyes both compete for your attention**, and your gaze flickers between the two pairs like an unresolvable duck-rabbit picture: "an arachnid *trompe l'œil*". Behind are four more eyes, like the gun-turret blisters of a Lancaster bomber.

The jumping spider family has about 5,000 species, smaller than a little fingernail:
- Some have sharper vision than a cat a hundred times their size, and their eight eyes together can scan a wide area
- Fine hairs on the legs sense the slightest vibration
- They can jump fifty times their body length, attaching a silk safety line before take-off

The author sums it up: a jumping spider is **a voracious panopticon, bungee-jumper and traceur in one**. In courtship males are extravagantly coloured, some with palps like bird-of-paradise plumes, and perform dances in three or even seven acts combining semaphore, flamenco and South African gumboot dancing.

points.h: *Portia*: a ninja on a slow download
points.body:
The plainest-looking genus, *Portia*, contains the cleverest species. *Portia labiata* eats only other spiders: it deceives them by imitating the rhythms that other species tap on a web; when a frontal attack is too dangerous, it spends an hour or more scanning the plants and gaps between itself and its prey to plan a roundabout route.

Scientists think it is slow because its capacity to process information is very limited, so it can only scan one small patch at a time, **like downloading a large picture over a very slow connection**. Once the map is built it almost never fails; if it takes a wrong turn it quickly doubles back, and finally drops on its prey like a special-forces ninja. (The only known vegetarian jumping spider is *Bagheera kiplingi*, named after the black panther in *The Jungle Book*.)

points.h: Narrow vision may be an advantage
points.body:
The human brain, too, is flooded with sensory information at every moment, and much of its work is **deciding what to ignore**. The narrow focus of *Portia*'s eyes does a lot of filtering for it, so its seemingly clever decisions may come simply from being less distracted by irrelevant information.

Humans have about a hundred billion neurons and jumping spiders six hundred thousand, and we also cooperate to weave webs far more powerful than any individual. But like them we live in a narrow band. In Stanisław Lem's *Solaris*: "Man can take in only very little at a time; we see only what is happening in front of us, here and now."

points.h: Memory is the foundation of life
points.body: If memory is defined as storing information for later use, it is the foundation of life itself: the first RNA world depended on it. Your cells replay, every moment, programs that date back to the Archaean. Most memory in the world is unconscious and does not even need a brain: the immune system "remembers" pathogens you have met, and plants remember too.

Borges's Funes gains a "perfect" memory after falling from a horse: he remembers the shapes of the clouds in the southern sky on the morning of 30 April 1882 and can compare them with the marbled binding of a book he saw only once. But he is bedridden from then on and **cannot generalize or abstract, because abstraction requires forgetting, a little at a time**.

- Théodule Ribot: forgetting is not a disease of memory but a condition of its health and life
- Thomas Browne: not knowing future evils and forgetting past ones is a merciful provision of nature
- Nietzsche: **blessed are the forgetful, for they also get over their stupidities**

Hume realized long ago, and neuroscience confirms, that remembering is re-creation: "true" memories turn into stories, and stories turn into "memories".

points.h: Looking back and forth between the present and memory
points.body:
Some of our most treasured experiences hold a tension: we want to live fully in the present (Wittgenstein: only someone who lives not in time but in the present is happy), and also to build and keep as complete a picture of the world as we can (Collingwood: history and memory are "the mind's triumph over time").

The author says some of life's most important moments are bridges between these two states, **just as we shift our attention back and forth between the jumping spider's two pairs of front eyes**. That "face" is blank and does not tell us where to look; and, like the cat in Kafka's "A Little Fable", it would eat us if it could.

expressions.en: an arachnid trompe l’œil
expressions.zh: A *trompe l'œil* (French, "deceives the eye") is a painting so realistic it fools the viewer; the spider's face is an eight-legged optical illusion.

expressions.en: A jumping spider is a voracious panopticon, bungee-jumper and traceur in one.
expressions.zh: Three roles in one: a panopticon (an all-seeing surveillance structure) with an appetite, a bungee jumper with its silk line, and a *traceur*, a practitioner of parkour.

expressions.en: cowering timorous beasties
expressions.zh: Adapted from Robert Burns's "To a Mouse": "Wee, sleekit, cow'rin, tim'rous beastie" (small, sleek, cowering, timid creature).

expressions.en: for what girl can resist a boy who has technicolor genitals in the middle of his face?
expressions.zh: What female could resist a male with technicolour genitals in the middle of his face? (The male spider's palps double as mating organs.)

expressions.en: a combination of semaphore, flamenco and South African gumboot dancing
expressions.zh: The jumping spider's courtship dance as a mix of flag signalling, flamenco and South African gumboot dancing.

expressions.en: like trying to download a large and fine-grained picture over a very slow Internet connection
expressions.zh: *Portia* scans so slowly it is like downloading a huge, detailed image over a crawling connection.

expressions.en: especially when we have not had too much to drink
expressions.zh: Memory can be astonishing, "especially when we have not had too much to drink": a dry British aside.

expressions.en: Blessed are the forgetful: for they also get over their stupidities.
expressions.zh: Nietzsche, parodying the Beatitudes of the Sermon on the Mount: the forgetful are blessed because they can also leave their own follies behind.

expressions.en: You need only change your direction.
expressions.zh: From Kafka's "A Little Fable": a mouse complains that the world grows narrower, and the cat says "You only need to change your direction", then eats it. The chapter's ending echoes it.

questions: *Portia* makes better decisions precisely because its information processing is limited. In your creative work, have constraints ever led you to do better?
Funes remembers everything yet cannot think. In today's information overload, do you think forgetting is a skill that needs practice?
Living in the present or living in memory: which side are you on more often? Is there any activity that lets you feel both at once?

lede: When a nautilus dies it leaves a perfect logarithmic-spiral shell, like a resolved chord. From it the author draws three wonders: time (the discovery of deep time, the moon's changing distance), the buoyancy chamber (from seabed killer to nuclear submarine), and the crudest of eyes, the pinhole (from camera obscura to photography).

points.body: Few creatures leave beautiful remains: the twisted trunk of an ancient oak is like a vast, turbulent musical score, while the nautilus shell is **like a chord resolved**. The author first saw a broken nautilus shell on a sandbar of a small Indonesian island; it seemed like a three-dimensional object in a flat world, an omen from the deep. (The calm "before or after humans" was actually an illusion: the island was in a protected area, and beyond its boundary were many hungry people.)

In the Renaissance, fossil shells were thought either to have grown spontaneously in rock or to have been left by the Flood. In his secret notebooks Leonardo da Vinci observed that fossils lie in several layers, which one flood cannot explain, and that shells have growth lines and would have cracked the rock had they grown inside it.

More than a hundred and fifty years later Robert Hooke studied ammonites and found the only living thing like them: the nautilus, then rare in Europe. He boldly asserted that **there were once many species that can no longer be found, and there may be new species that did not exist at first**. This challenged head-on the doctrine that species are neither lost nor added. In 1788 John Playfair wrote: "The mind seemed to grow giddy by looking so far into the abyss of time." Erasmus Darwin's motto was "everything from shells".

The nautilus is not a descendant of the ammonites but of the older nautiloids, which appeared about 490 million years ago and evolved into some 2,500 species; only two genera remain today. It still lives in its shell, has a simple brain and compensates with up to ninety suckerless tentacles; its favourite food is lobster that has just moulted and is still soft.

The Ordovician orthocone shells were shaped like witches' hats or British traffic cones, some perhaps as long as a giraffe: "the pointy-headed aquanauts of the Ordovician". The baroque spines on the backs of some trilobites may have been there to make them hard to swallow.

In the Ordovician, Earth spun faster: a day was 21 hours and a year 417 days; the moon was closer and tides were bigger. Today's nautilus lays down a fine line each day in step with the lunar tides, about 29 per chamber, exactly one lunar month. **The older the fossil, the fewer the lines**: Ordovician ones have only eight or nine, which means a month then was only a little longer than a week today.

Later the ammonites took over, and over 335 million years explored almost every form that can "grow by accretion", including the wildly irregular *Nipponites*. They survived the end-Permian extinction and finally, at the end of the Cretaceous, "joined the choir invisible".

In *Cosmicomics*, Qfwfq is a mollusc trapped in an eternal present, with days and nights crashing over him like identical waves. He starts building a shell, hoping to make himself a clock by spiral accretion and create an infinitely long time, but at a certain point the shell stops growing.

He realizes that **someone else** must turn all that is left behind into signs of something else. That is us: joining countless broken spiral shells into one continuous spiral called the history of the Earth. **The geological record is something other species lived through but only humans know.**

points.h: The buoyancy chamber: death from above, death from below
points.body:
The chambers inside a nautilus shell regulate gas and liquid through the siphuncle to control buoyancy. Long before fish evolved swim bladders, nautiloids could hover effortlessly above the seabed and move by jetting water from a siphon, becoming **the first great death from above**.

Humans had their first submarine using water tanks to dive and surface only in 1775: the *Turtle*, wobbly and a complete failure in combat. The submarine Robert Fulton built for the French Republic was called *Nautilus*; Jules Verne later used the name, and in 1954 the first nuclear submarine was named *Nautilus* too. A single submarine carrying intercontinental missiles can destroy the great cities of a whole continent: **from wobbly beginnings to the ultimate twenty-first-century "death from below"**. There were other dreams as well: the Catalan utopian socialist Narcís Monturiol built submarines to save coral divers.

In contrast to the mantis shrimp, the nautilus has the simplest eye of any large animal: **a pinhole without a lens**, able to distinguish only day from night and large objects. In spatial resolution it is worse than a horseshoe crab and less than a hundredth as good as a goldfish. It finds food mainly by smell. But eyes like this have been dimly watching the world for nearly five hundred million years, and they can serve as a point of reference for our own "artificial eyes".

Mozi and his disciples built a "locked treasure room" in which light came through a small hole onto a dark wall: the first camera obscura. (Mozi taught logic, self-knowledge and universal love, and his writings were once vigorously suppressed.)

points.h: Taking a moment out of time
points.body:
At thirteen the author made a pinhole camera from a tin can and photographed the twin towers of Westminster Abbey. Developing it the next day under cloud, he felt that **real photons from that day had left a lasting mark**, and Heraclitus's "everything flows" seemed not entirely right.
- Niépce's *View from the Window* of 1825 was exposed for more than eight hours, with sunlight and shadow falling on both sides: the moment is both a second and eight hours
- In Daguerre's *Boulevard du Temple* of 1838 the passers-by are ghosts, leaving only a man having his shoes shined and the shoeshiner: **the first humans ever photographed**, what Barthes called the *punctum*
- In 1843 Hill placed his hand on his daughter's head to keep her still during the long exposure; he could not prevent her early death. Susan Sontag: photographs testify to the innocence and vulnerability of lives heading toward their own destruction

Imaging technology lets us see that the world is always changing, and also makes us feel that a snapshot is everything. But on the true scale of things, we conscious beings see little better than a nautilus drifting in dark water under dim moonlight, **until we are cast up on a shoal of time**.

expressions.en: The oak is like a massive, turbulent musical score; the Nautilus shell is like a chord resolved.
expressions.zh: The oak is like a huge, surging musical score; the nautilus shell is like a chord that has resolved: tension released into rest.

expressions.en: no trace on the Rhodian shore
expressions.zh: From an ancient Greek story: the philosopher Aristippus, shipwrecked on the shore of Rhodes, saw geometric figures drawn in the sand and said "I see traces of men." The author means this shell is neither a token from God nor a trace of human design.

expressions.en: E conchis omnia
expressions.zh: Erasmus Darwin's Latin motto, "everything from shells", which he even put on his family coat of arms.

expressions.en: the pointy-headed aquanauts of the Ordovician
expressions.zh: The pointed-shelled seafarers of the Ordovician; *pointy-headed* is also American slang for a bookish intellectual.

expressions.en: Nothing so odd will do long.
expressions.zh: Dr Johnson's verdict on *Tristram Shandy*: nothing so odd will last long. Here applied to the bizarrely coiled *Nipponites*.

expressions.en: in an almighty prang … they joined the choir invisible
expressions.zh: *Prang* is British slang for a crash; "joined the choir invisible" comes from Monty Python's "Dead Parrot" sketch, one of its many euphemisms for being dead.

expressions.en: the first great death from above
expressions.zh: Nautiloids as the earliest killers striking from above; the chapter later pairs this with nuclear submarines as "death from below".

expressions.en: And then we were allowed out (!)
expressions.zh: "And then we were allowed out (!)": the author's wry aside on how strict his school was at the time.

expressions.en: cast up, lifeless, on a shoal of time
expressions.zh: Adapted from *Macbeth*'s "this bank and shoal of time": washed up, lifeless, on the shallows of time.

questions: A photograph can be both "a second" and "eight hours". In music, is there a similar experience of compressing a span of time into a single moment?
Calvino says "someone else" must turn what is left behind into signs. Do you think a work's meaning is given by its creator, or by those who come later?
In an age when digital imaging can conjure realistic pictures out of nothing, does the photograph still have an "aura"?

lede: Eight arms with fifty million neurons each, three hearts, blue blood, and a skin that can change both colour and texture. Octopus intelligence evolved entirely independently of ours. Henderson surveys the octopus monsters of the human imagination, then invites us to take the animal as a mentor.

points.body:
Textbooks say an octopus's limbs are "arms": not legs, and certainly not tentacles. Henderson prefers "super-tongues". Each arm is a tongue-like muscular hydrostat, and each sucker carries some ten thousand chemoreceptors (taste buds) and as many touch-sensitive nerve endings. Next time someone shows off by touching their nose with their tongue, tell them: **an octopus has eight tongues growing out of its cheeks, and it can double or halve their length at will.**

Each arm holds fifty million neurons, making it more like an extendable brain, or a semi-autonomous "body-brain" network. Working together they can squeeze the whole body through a gap no wider than an eyeball or beak, unscrew a jar, and in the big species, defeat a small shark.

points.h: The closer you look, the more there is
points.body:
Like the Mandelbrot set, the octopus reveals more the closer you look: the scrotum-like "head" can produce the full spectrum of colours; there are three hearts, and the blood uses copper instead of iron; the eyes are strikingly similar to ours, but more elegantly designed.

Its intelligence is at least on a par with a dog's. It can remember symbols on doors that hide crabs, discriminating symbols nearly as well as a three- or four-year-old child; **it can learn a maze by watching another octopus do it**; and it plays with balls dropped into its tank, for want of any other word. Yet our last common ancestor may have been a slug-like creature more than 540 million years ago. We are more closely related to starfish and sea cucumbers.

- The largest are the size of a car; the smallest adults are just 2.5 cm
- Female blanket octopuses outweigh males ten thousand times: "mating requires imagination as well as technique"
- Octopuses near hydrothermal vents look like a bleached Marge Simpson
- The deep-sea *Stauroteuthis* glows and spreads a pink web, probably the world's only "bathypelagic tutu"
- Dumbo octopuses live three to four kilometres down
- The blue-ringed octopus is only a few inches across, yet one of the most venomous animals on earth
- The mimic octopus can become a flatfish, a sea snake or a lionfish; the stripes of *Wunderpus photogenicus* are nature's answer to the op art of Bridget Riley
- The glass octopus is almost entirely transparent, aspiring to look like nothing at all

By comparison our cultural imagination is impoverished: the octopus is either a dish, a horror-film monster, Japanese soft porn, or World Cup entertainment.

Minoan octopus images still seem almost to burst into song 3,500 years later. After that, in the Mediterranean imagination, the octopus played a supporting role: Homer used it as a simile for Odysseus at his most wretched, and Scylla's six heads with triple rows of teeth may have come from the giant squid.

Pliny the Elder tells of an octopus that climbed a tree and over a fence to steal salted fish from a fish farm, and was finally killed with a trident; its arms were nearly thirty feet long. It sounds like a Roman version of the alligators in New York's sewers, but the behaviour is partly credible: **octopuses do slip out of aquarium tanks to eat the crabs next door and then slip back into their own, looking as innocent as lambs**, and sometimes only hidden cameras catch them in the act.

Linnaeus included the Nordic Kraken in the 1735 edition of *Systema Naturae*, and Bishop Pontoppidan said it was as big as a floating island. The giant squid was not accepted by biologists as real until 1857.

The French conchologist Montfort invented a story of a giant octopus sinking a British warship. When the hoax was exposed his reputation was ruined, but his image inspired Tennyson's sonnet and countless horror monsters.

In Victor Hugo's *Toilers of the Sea* the octopus is "a mystery of evil, a viscosity with a will". Hugo writes with wild exaggeration and terrible anatomy: "The tiger can only devour you; the octopus, horror, **inhales** you! ... Beyond the terror of being eaten alive is the ineffability of being drunk alive."

The most famous octopus of the twenty-first century was Paul, a common octopus at a provincial German aquarium. During the 2010 World Cup he chose between two boxes bearing national flags and "predicted" the winner every time. Spain's prime minister offered him state protection, and Iran's president Ahmadinejad said he proved Western decadence.

Apart from showing that German zoologists have a better sense of humour than conservative Iranian politicians, Henderson says, this showed that **an octopus can capture the popular imagination without being a monster**. Perhaps one day people will see how extraordinary the common octopus is without the wrapping of prophecy and football.

Mark Twain said man is the only animal that blushes, or needs to. He was only half right: **octopuses can blush in any of a dozen colours.** They open and close tens of thousands of pigment cells, matching continuous changes in their surroundings exactly, while distorting their skin in three dimensions to mimic the texture of rock or coral. This feat of perception and control exceeds anything humans can do with their bodies; only our symbolic realms of language and art compare.

The virtual-reality pioneer Jaron Lanier says that by rights **they should be running the world and we should be their pets**. The reason they are not is lifespan: the common octopus usually lives less than a year, and even the largest live only three to five years, often dying before their young hatch. They have no culture and no childhood guided by parents; every generation starts from scratch.

Lanier thinks the octopus's way of "embodying meaning" in its skin could inspire a future "post-symbolic communication". As early as 1567 Montaigne said we have built our truth from five senses, and perhaps it would take the agreement of eight or ten senses to know truth's real nature.

Medieval thinkers held that every land animal had a counterpart in the sea. Henderson suggests our counterpart may be not the dolphin but the octopus: let us take it as **a mentor in escapology, adaptability and self-expression**, and an ambassador for the idea that "it is never too late to have a happy childhood".

expressions.en: something that happens to me disturbingly often
expressions.zh: Someone shows off touching their nose with their tongue in front of him, "something that happens to me disturbingly often". A deadpan aside.

expressions.en: probably the world’s only bathypelagic tutu
expressions.zh: *Bathypelagic* is the ocean zone roughly one to four kilometres down; pairing that technical term with *tutu* (a ballet skirt) makes the comic image of the pink webbed *Stauroteuthis*.

expressions.en: nature’s answer to the op art of Bridget Riley
expressions.zh: The stripes of the Wunderpus as a natural reply to Bridget Riley, the British painter of dizzying black-and-white optical (op) art.

expressions.en: as innocent as lambs . . . or T.S. Eliot’s Macavity, the mystery cat
expressions.zh: Octopuses back in their tanks after a raid, looking as innocent as lambs, or like Macavity in T.S. Eliot's *Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats*, the criminal cat who is never at the scene of the crime.

expressions.en: a sundae of bizarre imaginings topped with a few accuracies
expressions.zh: A dessert metaphor for early accounts of the octopus: mostly fantasy, with a few true facts sprinkled on top like nuts on an ice-cream sundae.

expressions.en: a viscosity with a will
expressions.zh: Hugo's phrase for the octopus: a slime with a mind of its own.

expressions.en: Beyond the terror of being eaten alive is the ineffability of being drunk alive.
expressions.zh: Hugo's climax: worse than being eaten alive is the unspeakable horror of being drunk alive. *Ineffability* means the quality of being beyond words.

expressions.en: great works of art such as the film Mega Shark Versus Giant Octopus
expressions.zh: Heavy irony: calling a B-movie creature feature a "great work of art".

expressions.en: Man is the only animal that blushes – or needs to.
expressions.zh: Mark Twain's quip: we are the only animal that blushes, and the only one with reason to be ashamed.

expressions.en: it is never too late to have a happy childhood
expressions.zh: A line usually credited to the novelist Tom Robbins. Octopuses have no childhood at all, so Henderson turns it around to close the chapter.

questions: Octopuses are clever but have no cultural inheritance; each generation starts from zero. What would we be like if humans were the same?
Lanier imagines a post-symbolic communication that "embodies meaning" the way an octopus changes colour. Do your audio-reactive visual works count as a step in that direction?
What would it feel like to have a mind made of eight semi-autonomous "brains"? Can you imagine it?

lede: The shortest chapter in the book: the comic yet ferocious pufferfish, and its relative the ocean sunfish, inflated to two tonnes. In the old manner of the medieval bestiary, Henderson draws two lessons about humans from the puffer: our own odd appearance, and our runaway appetites.

points.body: Balloonfish, blowfish, bubblefish, globefish: pufferfish once sat in half the cabinets of curiosities of Renaissance Europe. Today they live in aquariums, but attitudes have hardly changed. They look comic, a bit ugly, a bit ridiculous, like Bloat in *Finding Nemo*, who swells up like an automatic life jacket whenever he is startled. **Even dolphins see them this way: they deliberately provoke puffers and, once they inflate, toss them about in a game of water polo.**

The order Tetraodontiformes has about 360 species, named for four teeth fused into a beak. They gave up the streamlined, flexible bodies of most fish and became rigid: spherical, box-shaped or triangular. They move by sculling with tail and side fins (ostraciiform locomotion), as if a person walked by turning only their feet and swam by paddling only their fingers and toes.

The reason is their niche. Some forty million years ago their ancestors began grazing on coral, and **hovering like a hummingbird mattered more than swimming far**: it let them find the best angle to bite off hard coral and algal crusts with their ever-growing beaks.

- The stomach rapidly fills with water, puffing the fish into a near-sphere that most fish cannot swallow
- In many species the spines can pierce the throat of a large animal such as a turtle, and sometimes the puffer **eats its way out from the inside**
- Many species contain tetrodotoxin, the same poison as the blue-ringed octopus
- Young puffers start biting their siblings as soon as their first teeth appear, and the extra food makes these cannibals grow faster and more agile

points.h: The sunfish: a drifting giant head
points.body: At least one tetraodontiform has left the reef altogether. **The ocean sunfish** is a pufferfish blown up to astonishing size: one or two tonnes and 3.3 metres across, the heaviest bony fish in the world. Before humans arrived it was too big to have predators, basking alone at the surface and feasting on salps, siphonophores and jellyfish. It looks like a head without a body, with a frill inexplicably attached behind and two misplaced wings or sails sticking out above and below.

points.h: First thought: we look strange too
points.body: We no longer treat animals as emblems of virtue and vice the way medieval writers did, Henderson says, but looking at puffers and sunfish still sets off certain associations. The first is our own oddness. Most cultures celebrate human beauty, yet we have knobbly ears, fast-changing faces and oversized heads tottering on improbably vertical bodies, and **sometimes we look utterly without grace**.

points.h: Second thought: appetite out of control
points.body:
In a world where hundreds of millions are obese and chefs keep inventing new things to eat (penis restaurants in China, competitive eating leagues in the United States, fritters made from live bears' paws in Southeast Asia), puffer prepared by a Japanese chef is still the ultimate challenge. The thrill is that the flesh keeps just enough poison to numb the lips: **one slip by the chef and the diner may die**.

The psychoanalyst Adam Phillips says: "The excessive appetite we call greed is really a form of despair... It is not that our appetites are excessive, but that our fear of frustration is." Our excesses are "the best clue we have to our sense of our own poverty, and the best way we have of concealing it from ourselves". We look for a remedy that will make us better and stronger, and often end up like Homer Simpson, who eats badly prepared fugu, resolves to spend his last hours living righteously and kindly, and fails completely at every item.

"Without virtue, man is the most unholy and the most savage of animals, and the most full of lust and gluttony." Unless we learn to manage our appetites more wisely and creatively, Henderson says, we will leave ourselves, the oceans and much else hugely impoverished, and **then we won't even have the Pufferfish left to wonder and laugh at**.

expressions.en: Men are troubled not by things, but by their opinions about things.
expressions.zh: The chapter epigraph from Epictetus (also the motto of *Tristram Shandy*): what troubles us is not things but our opinions about them. A hint that the puffer's "comic" look is our opinion, not its nature.

expressions.en: inflates as suddenly as an automatic life jacket
expressions.zh: An apt simile: the puffer swells as instantly as a life jacket that inflates on contact with water.

expressions.en: the dolphin version of water polo
expressions.zh: Dolphins batting an inflated puffer around as if it were a ball in a water-polo match.

expressions.en: Nimble nibblers
expressions.zh: "Agile little nibblers": a playful alliterative label for coral-grazing puffers.

expressions.en: the Puffer may then literally eat its way out
expressions.zh: *Literally* is meant literally here: the swallowed puffer may chew its way out through the predator's body.

expressions.en: snarfing salps, siphonophores and jellyfish
expressions.zh: *Snarf* is American slang for wolfing food down greedily, and the prey that follow (*salps, siphonophores*) carry on the alliteration on s.

expressions.en: oversized heads tottering on improbably vertical bodies
expressions.zh: A self-mocking picture of the human body: big heads wobbling on bodies balanced so improbably upright.

expressions.en: the hero with a thousand vices
expressions.zh: Homer Simpson as "the hero with a thousand vices", a parody of Joseph Campbell's *The Hero with a Thousand Faces*.

expressions.en: we won’t even have the Pufferfish to wonder and to laugh at
expressions.zh: The closing line: if we lose the sea's riches we lose even the chance to marvel at, and laugh at, the puffer.

questions: Phillips says greed is a form of despair, an excessive fear of frustration. Do you agree? Where have you had "excessive" appetites?
The thrill of eating fugu lies in the risk of death. Why do people seek out dangerous pleasures like this?
Henderson says humans sometimes look "utterly without grace". Why do you think we find certain animals funny?

lede: *Quetzalcoatlus*, of the Late Cretaceous, stood as tall as a giraffe and had the wingspan of a Spitfire, yet weighed about as much as a heavyweight boxer. Henderson uses it to show how hard flight is and how strange pterosaurs were, then turns to the human dream of flight, its wars and its ecstasies.

points.body:
Humans are picayune compared with elephants or whales, but giants compared with almost every flying animal. Richard Dawkins's thought experiment: shrink a hippo a thousandfold to the size of a flea. Its weight falls to a billionth but its surface area only to a millionth, so relative to its weight it has a thousand times more surface, and **a flea-sized hippo could float off easily on a puff of wind**.

Animal cells can produce only so much power, so the biggest fliers are astonishingly light:
- The golden-crowned flying fox has a 1.5-metre wingspan but weighs just 1.2 kg. It is hunted to the edge of extinction because it tastes good (in the Philippines Henderson met a seventeen-year-old crack shot called Stalin, who later really did go to Iraq as a sniper)
- The great bustard is the heaviest living flying bird; in the breeding season it grows feather "whiskers", like Victorian gentlemen gone slightly awry
- The wandering albatross can have a wingspan of 3.5 metres

The California condor was once down to fewer than two dozen birds, most deaths caused by electrocution on power lines. Los Angeles Zoo uses condor hand puppets to teach chicks to avoid the lines, and Henderson was warned to keep out of sight, because **if the chicks see a human they fall hopelessly in love with you**.

points.h: From bones in a cabinet to "wing fingers"
points.body:
In 1757 someone found a pile of unidentified bones in a cabinet of curiosities at the Mannheim palace. Voltaire's former secretary thought they belonged to a sea creature that paddled with its forelimbs. In 1801 Cuvier correctly judged the "paddles" to be **enormously elongated fingers** supporting the wings of a flying reptile, and named it the pterodactyl, "wing finger". In 1971 the largest *Quetzalcoatlus* yet known was found in a Texas quarry.

Pterosaurs preceded the first birds by some 45 million years and the first bats by about 150 million: they were **the first vertebrates to master flight**.

From small insect-eaters in the Triassic skies to eaters of fish and crustaceans, there were more than a hundred species of pterosaur, ranging from blackbird size to light-aircraft size.
- The short-winged, big-headed *Dimorphodon*, and *Anurognathus*, the "fantastic flying frog head"
- *Rhamphorhynchus*, with a diamond-shaped vane at the end of its long tail
- The albatross-like *Ornithocheirus*, with a 7-metre wingspan
- The plankton-eating *Pterodaustro*, possibly pink
- Finally the azhdarchids, named after a dragon of Uzbek myth, including *Quetzalcoatlus*

Then nothing. In the film *One Million Years B.C.* a *Pteranodon* snatches up Raquel Welch and is then attacked by a *Rhamphorhynchus*. Not quite historically accurate, Henderson notes: the two are fifty million years apart, "and Raquel Welsh is not nearly that old".

points.h: If your ring finger became a wing
points.body:
Imagine your ring finger grew longer than your whole arm and hand, and stretched a wing membrane from its tip to your shoulder and down to your knee. Your bones are full of air spaces like polystyrene foam, with walls as thin as a credit card; an extra bone juts from your wrist to support a membrane along the leading edge; and your whole body is covered in hair like a grown man's forearm.

The cliché of the lumbering leather-winged glider is the opposite of the truth. The membrane contained hundreds of fibre strips whose tension was adjusted by voluntary muscles, and proprioceptors sent information many times a second to a **flocculus proportionally larger than in any other animal**. They could reshape their wings instantly, something the most advanced military researchers can only dream of, and in their sense of body position they may have been as acute as tai chi masters. On the ground they scuttled on all fours, like saddle-sore cowboys walking on crutches.

The crest of *Pteranodon* resembles the pointed hood of a Spanish penitent or the Ku Klux Klan; the crest of Brazil's *Tupandactylus* was five times the height of its skull, like the greatest of African masks. In 1856 the *Illustrated London News* joked that a live pterodactyl had flown out of the rock during tunnelling in France, and in 1925 the film of Arthur Conan Doyle's *The Lost World* became **the first in-flight movie**.

Cryptozoologists have recorded the African "kongamato", which specialises in overturning canoes, "so long as there were no cameras about". Creationists say pterosaurs were vegetarians in Eden and turned carnivore only after the Fall, and that the Israelites in the wilderness, without ibises to protect them, were plagued by pterosaurs. The Chinese dragon has the antlers of a deer, the head of a camel, the eyes of a demon, the belly of a clam-monster, the scales of a fish, the talons of an eagle, the paws of a tiger and the ears of an ox.

Some proposed that birds and mammals share a common ancestor (warm blood surely couldn't evolve twice? In fact it did). Others put forward a "flying primate" theory: that our ancestors flew before they leapt. Both were rejected.

The "flier" more closely related to us than bats are is Southeast Asia's colugo, which can glide 150 metres and looks in the air like a furry bath mat. Madagascar's crowned sifaka has a furry membrane on its arms like the trailing edge of an aerofoil; one zoologist thinks it resembles an early stage in the evolution of the bird wing. But its forests are disappearing fast.

In 852 Ibn Firnas of Córdoba jumped from a minaret wearing a winged cloak. Twenty-five years later he flew a stretch in a home-made glider and turned back, then crashed: he had not learned how birds slow down before landing.

A contrast that reads like a fable: Santos-Dumont, a rich young Brazilian, believed aviation would bring peace and prosperity to all humanity and **released the design of his Demoiselle monoplane free to the public**. The Wright brothers guarded their patents and were eager to sell the aeroplane to the US government for war. Santos-Dumont lost. The air war of the First World War sank him into depression, and he finally hanged himself, "making practical use, with a noose, of the gravity he had so long defied". The mass air raids and atomic bombs H.G. Wells foretold later came true.

Saint-Exupéry said the aeroplane "abolished the time and space that separate us" and helped humans understand one another. Cheap flights let the top billion of humanity enjoy beautiful views, crowded beaches and drunken weekends abroad, but air power also guards oilfields, and aviation emissions are driving the fastest change in atmospheric composition in millions of years.

The art group Platform says: from a North Sea oilfield to a 747 over the Atlantic, **it takes only ten days for geology formed 57 million years ago to be burned into gas**. We don't know how much time is left on the clock, or whether it ends in a soft landing or a bang. As for green aviation fuel, Henderson says: "Seeing is believing."

Saint-Exupéry: **perfection is achieved not when there is nothing more to add, but when there is nothing left to take away**. Wingsuit fliers are the modern heirs of Ibn Firnas: jumping from a cliff, they reach terminal velocity within nine seconds, open the suit at about the sixth second, and glide at a ratio of about 2.5 to 1. Karina Hollekim broke her legs in twenty-five places and lost three-quarters of her blood, but she has no regrets: "It forces you to feel... in the air, it's like being in love."

After a crash landing in the Sahara, Saint-Exupéry lay on his back in the sand and, half awake, thought he was falling into the stars. In fact we are all falling: the Earth "falls" around the Sun at 30 kilometres a second. True flight with our own bodies will probably always be a dream, Henderson says, and **this is literally our "ground truth"**. Recognising our limits lets us appreciate other animals' flight all the more, and remember that creatures as heavy as us really did once take to the sky.

expressions.en: Humans are picayune compared to elephants or whales
expressions.zh: *Picayune* was once a small coin in the American South; by extension it means trivial or tiny.

expressions.en: Of course, we might not notice it passing.
expressions.zh: A dry punchline to the shrunken-hippo thought experiment: a flea-sized hippo drifting past on the breeze would probably escape our notice.

expressions.en: like Victorian gentlemen gone slightly awry
expressions.zh: The bustard's feather whiskers, like a Victorian gentleman's side-whiskers slightly gone to seed.

expressions.en: if the chicks see a human they fall hopelessly in love with you
expressions.zh: Condor chicks that see a person imprint on them and fall hopelessly in love, which is why keepers hide behind puppets.

expressions.en: like a giant version of Suppen-Kaspar
expressions.zh: Suppen-Kaspar is the boy in the German children's book *Struwwelpeter* who refuses his soup and wastes away to a thread.

expressions.en: Raquel Welsh is not nearly that old
expressions.zh: "Raquel Welch isn't nearly that old": a joke about the film putting two pterosaurs fifty million years apart in one scene. (Henderson's text spells the name *Welsh* here.)

expressions.en: pterosaurs were ptoast
expressions.zh: "Pterosaurs were toast" (finished), with a silent p added to *toast* to mimic the spelling of *pterosaur*.

expressions.en: like saddle-sore cowboys walking on crutches
expressions.zh: Pterosaurs on the ground: like cowboys hobbling on crutches, sore from too long in the saddle.

expressions.en: so long as there were no cameras about
expressions.zh: A sly dig at eyewitness reports of cryptids: the creature appears only when no one has a camera.

expressions.en: he had walked through life as money’s guest
expressions.zh: He went through life as money's guest: born rich, he never had to worry about money.

expressions.en: making practical use, with a noose, of the gravity he had so long defied
expressions.zh: Grim irony: Santos-Dumont, who spent his life defying gravity, used it to hang himself.

expressions.en: This is, literally, our ground truth.
expressions.zh: *Ground truth* is a remote-sensing term for data checked on the ground; here a pun: the truth is that we are bound to the ground.

questions: Santos-Dumont chose to give his design away; the Wright brothers chose patents and military sales. In technology and in art, what does openness cost, and what does protection cost?
Hollekim says she can feel intense emotion only in the air. Have you had a similar experience of being truly alive only while doing one particular thing?
Henderson says recognising our limits helps us appreciate other things better. What does that mean for a creator?

lede: Off Svalbard, a musician on board the ship lowered a hydrophone and picked up a seal's long, haunting whistle. Only later did Henderson realise that what deserved attention was an absence: three hundred years ago, seal calls here were just the background to the songs of thousands of whales. The right whale's name says it all: it was the "right" whale to kill, because it was easy.

points.body:
Light on the sea's surface is mesmerising, but sound underwater is something else: it reveals unseen space, the way rain on forest leaves or bells echoing across a hillside paint a landscape for a blind person. The whistle slid slowly down from on high, like a swanee whistle or a theremin but richer and sweeter, and **we were no longer bobbing on a steel-grey sea but seemed to float in an airship above a hidden world**.

John Muir: all things make music with their lives.

In the 1960s the biologist Roger Payne first heard whale sounds recorded by the US Navy: "like walking into a darkened cave and hearing wave after wave of echoes cascading back... That's what whales do, give the ocean its voice." He and his colleagues found that humpback sounds are not repeated at random like a dog's barks but form **rhythmic, precisely repeated sequences**: true songs.

The 1970 album *Songs of the Humpback Whale* sold over thirty million copies, became the best-selling nature recording of the twentieth century and the soundtrack of the environmental movement, and was included on the Voyager Golden Record of 1977. Carl Safina says we feel differently about whales than about fish not because they have the largest brains in the known universe but because **their songs touch the singing centres of our own brains. It's not intellect, it's soul.**

Right whales are slow, stay near the coast, are easy to kill, and float when dead, so they can be towed ashore. They are packed with blubber, oil, meat and baleen, all valuable commodities. Humans hunted them to the edge of extinction.

There are four species: the North Atlantic, North Pacific and southern right whales, and the bowhead. They are 11 to 17 metres long, longer than an old London double-decker bus, and can weigh 65 tonnes. The mouth curves up and forward from below the eye, like a scar across a pirate's face, and hundreds of baleen plates taller than a person filter copepods and krill like a comb. The white **callosities** on the head are caused by parasitic crustaceans, "whale lice".

Apart from humans and the killer whales that occasionally take calves, right whales lead a leisurely life: snacking, singing, sleeping and mating. Males compete not by fighting but by producing more sperm; each testicle can weigh half a tonne, the largest in the animal kingdom. Females calve once every three years: a year pregnant, a year nursing, a year resting.

The bowhead has the largest mouth on earth, with baleen three to four and a half metres long and a five-metre tongue; its skull is hard enough to smash through ice 60 cm thick. Males sing "whoop eroop, whoop eroop", using song to hold the group together in ice and darkness. They are extremely long-lived: in 1995 Iñupiat whalers in Alaska found two **stone harpoon heads** in the blubber of a bowhead, and stone tools had been replaced by metal more than a century earlier.

- The Bangudae petroglyphs in Korea (6000 to 1000 BC) show people hunting whales with harpoons and floats
- Around AD 800 the Thule culture hunted bowheads in open water, used whale ribs and jaws as house frames, and buried warriors among whale bones
- From the eleventh century the Basques whaled commercially in the Bay of Biscay; the English word *harpoon* may come from the Basque *arpoi*, "to take quickly"
- The Basques pursued whales as far as Labrador and Newfoundland; English colonists killed almost all of Massachusetts's 5,000 to 10,000 right whales in little more than a century

Medieval bestiaries said a whale could be mistaken for a floating island; sailors lit a fire on its back, and in pain it sank to the bottom of the sea.

There may once have been 70,000 to 100,000 southern right whales; by 1920 there were at most a few hundred, perhaps only twenty-five breeding females. Once protected, the survivors doubled their numbers every ten years (humans take thirty at the fastest). Seeing this rate of growth in the 1960s, the Soviets decided they could kill several thousand, roughly half the population, and **told the international authorities they had taken four**. Today there are more than 10,000 southern right whales, but only three or four hundred North Atlantic right whales.

About 150,000 whales were killed between 1770 and 1900, and more than three million in the twentieth century. The writer Philip Hoare estimates that in 1958, the year he was born, factory ships took more whales than in the entire 150-year era of American whaling that *Moby-Dick* represents.

William Scoresby described a mother sperm whale weaving among her enemies to protect her calf: "an affection for her young that would do honour to the superior intelligence of human beings... yet the object of the adventure, the value of the prize, the joy of the capture, cannot be sacrificed to feelings of compassion." Another record tells of the sea around a killed mother whale turning white with her milk, which unsettled even the crew.

Barry Lopez notes that a bowhead sleeping at the surface will start awake when a bird lands on its back; the whalers must have known how intense the pain of a harpoon was. In 1856 one whale ran out 1,200 yards of line in three and a half minutes, hit the seabed, broke its back, and buried its head eight feet deep in the mud.

We are happy to condemn small-scale whaling by Japan, Norway and others, but we should also face the larger threats for which we are responsible:
- Rerouting shipping lanes around feeding and breeding grounds has already helped North Atlantic right whales
- Reducing ship noise: whales once heard companions a thousand kilometres away, and **the area across which they can communicate has shrunk ten-thousandfold**
- Arctic summer sea ice may vanish in the 2030s; if extraction is not excessive and humans don't eat all the krill, this could become a new feeding ground for bowheads

In the Gulf of California, grey whales that were once ruthlessly hunted now approach humans of their own accord, communicating through eye contact and touch. Blue whales have ten times as many neurons as we do for receiving sound below 100 hertz. "**We are not finished with whales**," Hoare says, "and the remarkable thing is that the whales have not given up on us."

A young woman fell in love with a bowhead whale, and he became a man for her. They had children who were both human and whale, and she always told her descendants: "The sea gives us food, but remember that your whale brothers live there. Don't hunt them; protect them and sing to them."
