expressions.zh: From the Gospel of John ("the Word was made flesh"), used ironically of the cloned dog; the later *virgin birth* is the same kind of religious irony.

expressions.en: in the immortalist scenario, humans engineer their own extinction
expressions.zh: John Gray's point: the dream of uploading ourselves to live forever amounts to planning the end of humanity.

expressions.en: Handyman for the earth.
expressions.zh: Lewis Thomas's modest job description for humanity: not master of the planet but its odd-job man.

expressions.en: a form of prayer for the less deceived
expressions.zh: *The Less Deceived* is the title of a poetry collection by Philip Larkin; the phrase suggests prayer for those who have lost illusions.

questions: Henderson says watching with your own eyes under a microscope is better than speeded-up video on a computer. What irreplaceable role do you think "being there" plays in understanding and feeling?
"Play = pleasure + learning." How much of your music and visual work is "play"?
"Handyman for the earth" or "posthuman": which would you rather humanity become?

lede: The title is "A Conclusion, in which Nothing is Concluded". In the shortest chapter of the book, Henderson admits this bestiary can never be finished, but one thing is clearer than ever: we are fully human only when we act as if the life beyond us matters.

points.h: Even the best maps are like a medieval mappa mundi
points.body: This book has tried to understand and imagine "being" and "beings" a little better. Any progress it has made is owed to other people's insight and thought, above all to the scientific method, which Feynman called **the best way we have learned of keeping from fooling ourselves**. But our understanding of the world we are creating is still poor, and even the best maps and forecasts may be little more accurate than a medieval map of the world.

points.h: What kind of garden are we cultivating?
points.body:
The previous chapter quoted Candide's "we must cultivate our garden". But what kind of garden are we cultivating in the Anthropocene? What kinds of creatures will thrive in it? Karel Čapek joked that a true gardener would want to see "eleven hundred years" into the future in order to test, understand and fully appreciate what is his.

A few things are fairly certain. Humans will go on hugely influencing the Earth system; **the greenhouse gases we emit will very likely prevent an ice age due in the next 48,000 years**, and if we carry on as we are, perhaps every ice age in the next half million years. The next century or two will be bumpy unless we develop better systems for managing resources and pollution and for dealing with risk and conflict. Still, human creativity is almost limitless.

As soon as we try to predict precisely, all these factors become like Rorschach's ink blots: we can read almost (but not quite) anything we want into them. If the complexity of the Earth-human system means that much must remain unknowable, then we need, as two critics of transhumanism put it, to "**rehabilitate humility**". Only then can we hear the voices that are hard to hear, not just the ones we want to hear. As in the story of Oedipus, tragedy comes when we refuse to listen.

Writing this book over more than four years was like designing, building and towing a **juggernaut**: one of the huge wooden temple cars that carry Hindu gods, decorated with tier upon tier of roofs, images, banners and incense. Sometimes the whole thing nearly toppled over; sometimes great effort moved it only a little, and then it turned out to be going the wrong way.

The more he wrote, the clearer it became that the project could never be finished, as new wonders kept appearing. Martin Rees says: "The complex structures that living things embody make them far more mysterious than an atom or a star." But one thing is clearer than ever: **we are only fully human when we act as if the life beyond us matters**.

By the time the book was published, more than five years had passed since the picnic in the Introduction. Henderson has watched his daughter grow from a helpless baby into a clever, lively, lovely little girl. A placard at the 2011 Occupy Wall Street protests read: "**The beginning is nigh.**" (A play on the doom-mongers' favourite, "The end is nigh".) Henderson says he likes it: my daughter's world, and yours, is only just beginning.

expressions.en: A Conclusion, in which Nothing is Concluded
expressions.zh: The title borrows that of the last chapter of Samuel Johnson's novel *Rasselas*: an ending that deliberately refuses to sum things up.

expressions.en: the best way we have learned about how to keep from fooling ourselves
expressions.zh: Feynman's definition of the scientific method: the best tool we have found for not deceiving ourselves.

expressions.en: like Rorschach’s ink blots
expressions.zh: The Rorschach test asks people what they see in symmetrical ink blots; everyone reads in what they want to see.

expressions.en: ‘rehabilitate humility’
expressions.zh: To *rehabilitate* is to restore someone or something to good standing after disgrace; humility has fallen out of favour and needs its reputation restored.

expressions.en: design, build and tow a juggernaut
expressions.zh: *Juggernaut* comes from Jagannath, the deity whose enormous temple car is hauled through Puri in India; in English it came to mean an unstoppable, crushing force.

expressions.en: we are only fully human when we act as if the life beyond us matters
expressions.zh: The book's central conclusion: our humanity is completed only by taking other life seriously.

expressions.en: The beginning is nigh.
expressions.zh: A reversal of the street preacher's placard *The end is nigh*: instead of doom, a beginning.

questions: Having read the whole book, which animal struck you most as "barely imagined"?
"We are only fully human when we act as if the life beyond us matters." Do you agree? What does this mean in your life or creative work?
Henderson ends with "the beginning is nigh". After a book so full of extinction and crisis, do you feel more hope or more worry?
